answers.text: They turn themselves in to the police immediately.
They decide to run and seek help from a trusted older friend.
They go home and pretend nothing happened.
They ask Cherry Valance for help.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy and Johnny choose to flee and turn to an older friend for advice rather than face the immediate consequences.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the final pages of Chapter 4. What do Ponyboy and Johnny decide to do after the confrontation?

questions.text: In a story, a "signal" is best described as:

answers.text: A character's name that hints at the plot.
A chapter title that summarizes the events.
A conversation between two characters at the beginning.
A detail that foreshadows or hints at what is coming later in the story.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A signal is a detail the author places early so that when a big event arrives, it feels like it was building all along.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what you practiced this week: small details that hint at what is coming. What is the term for that kind of detail?

questions.text: Which of these best describes an analytical claim about a character?

answers.text: "Johnny is a greaser who lives in the same neighborhood as Ponyboy."
"In Chapter 4, something serious happens and the characters have to run."
"Ponyboy narrates the story in first person."
"Johnny's decision in Chapter 4 shows that his loyalty to Ponyboy is more powerful than his fear of consequences."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A claim takes a position about what a detail means. The other options describe facts or events without interpreting them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A claim is not a summary or a fact. It says what you think a detail or event reveals. Which option does that?

questions.text: The tension in Chapter 3 contributes to the crisis in Chapter 4. What does this pattern suggest about how the novel is structured?

answers.text: Events in this novel happen randomly, without any connection to each other.
The novel builds its big events gradually, using earlier scenes to prepare the reader.
Earlier events are not connected to what happens later.
Chapter 4 would make sense without reading Chapter 3 first.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The way Chapter 3 builds tension that erupts in Chapter 4 is an example of the novel's structure: earlier events prepare you for later ones.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the relationship between the chapters. Does Chapter 4 come out of nowhere, or does Chapter 3 set it up?

questions.text: Which word is the adverb in "The small crowd gathered quietly near the old fountain"?

answers.text: quietly
small
gathered
near

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Quietly" tells how the crowd gathered. It answers "how" about the verb, so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb "gathered" and ask "gathered how?" The word that answers that question is the adverb.

questions.text: Which sentence is in passive voice?

answers.text: The coach selected the starting lineup before the game.
My sister baked a birthday cake yesterday.
The decision was made by the committee.
A student left a backpack in the hallway.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Was made" is a helping verb plus a past-participle main verb, and the subject (decision) is receiving the action, not performing it. That is passive voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In passive voice the subject receives the action. Look for a helping verb before the main verb. Which sentence fits that pattern?

questions.text: The Outsiders is narrated in first person by Ponyboy. What does that mean for a reader who wants to understand all the characters fairly?

answers.text: We can trust everything Ponyboy says about every character completely.
The story is told by an outside narrator who knows everyone's thoughts.
Ponyboy's view is the only perspective in the novel, so we only see what he sees and understands.
The first-person narrator means the story happened exactly as written.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A first-person narrator shows us events through one character's eyes. That means Ponyboy's understanding, feelings, and limitations shape everything we know.
questions.feedback_incorrect: First person means one character narrates with "I." What does that mean for how much we can know about other characters?

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "The frightened boy hid silently behind the old wooden door."

Which part of the sentence is a prepositional phrase?

answers.text: The frightened boy
hid silently
behind the old wooden door
frightened boy hid

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "The dog barked, and the boys stayed still."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Fragment

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "Because the rain started, the two boys ran inside."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Run-on

questions.text: In the sentence "The restless boy read quietly," what part of speech is the word "quietly"?

answers.text: Adjective, because it describes something in the sentence
Adverb, because it answers "How?" about the verb
Preposition, because it comes after the verb
Noun, because it names something

questions.text: A student wrote: "Because she was tired." Can this stand alone as a complete sentence?

answers.text: Yes, because it has a subject and a verb
No, because it is a dependent clause that needs an independent clause to complete it
Yes, if you add a period at the end
No, because it has no subject

questions.text: In Chapters 5–6, where do Ponyboy and Johnny hide out while they wait for help?

answers.text: A barn on the edge of town
An abandoned church on a hill
Dally's apartment
A friend's basement

questions.text: Robert Frost's poem "Nothing Gold Can Stay" describes something beautiful and golden that cannot last. In the context of Chapters 5–6, what does "gold" most likely represent for Ponyboy?

answers.text: Actual gold or money
The greasers' loyalty to each other
Innocence, beauty, and the part of youth that cannot be held on to
The sunrise itself, and nothing more

questions.text: Which of the following best describes how Johnny changes during Chapters 5–6?

answers.text: He becomes more frightened and unable to function.
He turns against Ponyboy and wants to give himself up immediately.
He becomes calmer and more decisive, taking charge of practical decisions.
He spends the whole time sleeping.

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "Although the boys were hungry, they waited quietly."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Fragment

questions.text: In the sentence "He spoke softly to the nervous dog," what part of speech is the word "softly"?

answers.text: Adjective, because it describes the dog
Adverb, because it answers "How?" about the verb
Noun, because it follows the verb
Preposition, because it comes before a noun

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 4: Capitalization and Punctuation + Punctuating Titles and Quotations)

questions.text:
Which word in this sentence needs to be capitalized?

"Every wednesday, the boys met at the park."

answers.text: every
boys
wednesday
park

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Wednesday is the name of a specific day of the week, so it is a proper noun and must be capitalized.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that names a specific day, month, or proper noun. Days of the week are always capitalized.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly capitalizes the title used before a name?

answers.text: She spoke with officer Torres about the report.
She spoke with Officer Torres about the report.
She Spoke With officer Torres About The Report.
she spoke with officer torres about the report.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A title used directly before a person's name is capitalized: Officer Torres.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When a title comes right before a specific person's name, it is capitalized. When it stands alone, it is lowercase.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the correct end mark?

answers.text: Did the hospital allow visitors every day.
Did the hospital allow visitors every day?
Did the hospital allow visitors every day!
Did the hospital allow visitors every day;

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The sentence asks a question, so it ends with a question mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the purpose of the sentence. A sentence that asks something is interrogative and ends with a question mark.

questions.text:
Which word in this sentence should NOT be capitalized?

"Two boys from tulsa waited outside Memorial Hospital."

answers.text: Boys
tulsa (needs to be capitalized)
Boys
Memorial Hospital

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Boys is a common noun; it should not be capitalized in the middle of a sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Tulsa and Memorial Hospital are proper nouns and must be capitalized. Boys is a common noun used in the middle of a sentence: no capital letter needed.

questions.text: Which sentence uses title punctuation correctly for a novel?

answers.text: He had read "The Outsiders" twice.
He had read THE OUTSIDERS twice.
He had read The Outsiders twice.
He had read The Outsiders twice.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A novel is a long work and its title is italicized (or underlined in handwriting).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Long works like novels, films, and albums get italics (or underlining in handwriting). Quotation marks are for short works like poems and short stories.

questions.text: Which sentence uses title punctuation correctly for a poem?

answers.text: She memorized Nothing Gold Can Stay for class.
She memorized Nothing Gold Can Stay for class.
She memorized "Nothing Gold Can Stay" for class.
She memorized NOTHING GOLD CAN STAY for class.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A poem is a short work, so its title goes in quotation marks.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Short works like poems, short stories, and song titles go in quotation marks. Italics are for long works like novels and films.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly introduces a quotation with a signal phrase?

answers.text: The narrator recalls "I kept walking and did not look back." (Ch. 7)
The narrator recalls, "I kept walking and did not look back." (Ch. 7)
The narrator recalls. "I kept walking and did not look back." (Ch. 7)
The narrator recalls "I kept walking and did not look back" (Ch. 7).

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A comma follows the signal phrase before the opening quotation mark. The period goes inside the closing quotation mark, before the citation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A signal phrase is followed by a comma, then the opening quotation mark. The period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.text: Where does the period go when a sentence ends with a quoted passage?

answers.text: After the closing quotation mark, outside it.
Before the opening quotation mark.
Inside the closing quotation mark.
There is no period; the quotation mark ends the sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In American English, the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In American English, periods and commas always go inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.

questions.text: Which version correctly cites a quotation from Chapter 8?

answers.text: "He said nothing at all" (Ch. 8).
"He said nothing at all." (Ch. 8)
"He said nothing at all" (Ch. 8.)
He said nothing at all (Ch. 8).

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The period follows the parenthetical citation: close the quotation mark, then the citation, then the period.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The correct order is: closing quotation mark, then the citation in parentheses, then the period. The period does not go inside the quote when there is a citation following it.

questions.text: A sentence that gives a strong command ends with:

answers.text: A comma
A question mark
A semicolon
A period or an exclamation mark

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Imperative sentences (commands or requests) typically end with a period; when the command is urgent or emotional, an exclamation mark is correct.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A command is an imperative sentence. It ends with a period for a calm instruction or an exclamation mark for a forceful or urgent one.

questions.text: In Chapters 7 and 8 of The Outsiders, the story slows down and focuses on characters in the hospital. What best describes the main emotional tone of these chapters?

answers.text: Excited and triumphant
Tense and hopeful at the same time
Funny and relaxed
Angry and loud

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. These chapters balance fear, hope, and quiet loyalty as characters wait and worry.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the mood when characters are waiting at the hospital. It is not triumphant or relaxed.

questions.text: In The Outsiders, the theme of loyalty is mostly shown through:

answers.text: Characters winning fights
Characters staying with each other during hard times
Characters earning money
Characters running away from problems

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Loyalty in this novel shows up as presence and commitment, not victories.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about how loyalty is actually demonstrated in Chapters 7 and 8. It is not about winning.

questions.text: A theme in a story is best described as:

answers.text: A single exciting event in the plot
The setting where the story takes place
The main character's full name
An idea about life the story keeps returning to

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Theme is the big idea running through the whole story, not just one scene.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Theme is bigger than one event or a character's name. Think about what the story keeps saying about life.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence should be capitalized? "Every summer, the gang met at the park on friday evenings."

answers.text: summer
gang
park
friday

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Friday is the name of a specific day of the week, so it is a proper noun: capitalize it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Summer and park are common nouns used generally. Days of the week (Friday) are proper nouns and always capitalized.

questions.text: Which sentence uses title punctuation correctly?

answers.text: Ponyboy reads "The Outsiders" every night.
Ponyboy reads the outsiders every night.
Ponyboy reads The Outsiders every night.
Ponyboy reads THE OUTSIDERS every night.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A novel is a long work; its title is italicized (or underlined in handwriting).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Long works like novels use italics. Quotation marks are for short works like poems and stories.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly introduces a quotation with a signal phrase?

answers.text: The narrator explains "nobody moved for a long moment." (Ch. 7)
The narrator explains, "nobody moved for a long moment." (Ch. 7)
The narrator explains. "nobody moved for a long moment." (Ch. 7)
The narrator explains "nobody moved for a long moment" (Ch. 7).

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A comma follows the signal phrase, and the period goes inside the closing quotation mark before the citation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A signal phrase is followed by a comma, then the quotation. The period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a proper noun? "Officer Mitchell visited the boys at Memorial Hospital on Tuesday."

answers.text: officer
boys
hospital
Tuesday

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Tuesday names a specific day of the week, so it is a proper noun and is capitalized. (Mitchell, Memorial Hospital, and Officer Mitchell used as a title+name are also proper nouns.)
questions.feedback_incorrect: A proper noun names a specific person, place, day, or organization. Look for the word that names a specific day.

questions.text: Where does the period go when you end a sentence with a quoted passage?

answers.text: After the closing quotation mark
Before the opening quotation mark
Inside the closing quotation mark
There is no period; the quotation mark is enough

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. In American English, periods and commas always go inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In American English, the period belongs inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 5: Dialogue Punctuation and Correcting Dialogue)

questions.text:
Stem: Read the sentence below. Where does the comma belong?

"I finished the report" said Mr. Callahan.

Which version places the comma correctly?

answers.text: "I finished the report," said Mr. Callahan.
"I finished the report" said, Mr. Callahan.
"I finished the report", said Mr. Callahan.
,"I finished the report" said Mr. Callahan.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, directly after the last word of the spoken line, before the dialogue tag.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. When a dialogue tag follows the spoken words, the comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark. Look again at option (a).

questions.text:
Stem: A student wrote this sentence:

Elena shouted, "Watch out for the step."

Which statement correctly describes the punctuation in this sentence?

answers.text: The comma is in the wrong place; it should come after the quotation mark.
The period should be outside the quotation mark.
The sentence is correctly punctuated: comma after the dialogue tag introducer, spoken words in quotation marks, period inside the closing quotation mark.
The spoken words do not need quotation marks because a dialogue tag is already present.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. This is a speaker-at-end pattern. The comma follows the dialogue tag introducer, the spoken words are enclosed in quotation marks, and the period sits inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Read the sentence again. The comma follows the dialogue tag introducer correctly, the spoken words are inside quotation marks, and the period is inside the closing quotation mark. That is the correct form for this pattern.

questions.text: Stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

answers.text: "Let's leave early" she suggested.
"Let's leave early," she suggested.
"Let's leave early", she suggested.
"Let's leave early." she suggested.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark when a dialogue tag follows. Option (b) places it exactly right.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. When spoken words come first and a dialogue tag follows, the period at the end of the spoken line changes to a comma, and that comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.text:
Stem: Read this sentence:

Jordan replied, "The practice starts at four o'clock".

What is the error?

answers.text: The comma after "replied" should not be there.
The period is outside the closing quotation mark; it should be inside.
The spoken words do not need quotation marks.
"replied" should be capitalized.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In American English, the period always goes inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Look at where the period lands. In American English, a period at the end of a quoted sentence belongs inside the closing quotation mark, not after it.

questions.text:
Stem: A student wrote this sentence:

"Keep the door closed," she reminded us, "because the cat will escape."

Which statement correctly describes this sentence?

answers.text: This is an interrupted dialogue pattern. The spoken line is split by a dialogue tag, with a comma inside the first closing quotation mark and a lowercase letter starting the second part.
There are too many quotation marks; the second set should be removed.
The comma after "closed" should be a period because "she reminded us" ends a complete thought.
The second part of the spoken line should begin with a capital letter.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. This is the interrupted dialogue pattern. The dialogue tag splits the spoken line, so a comma closes the first part inside the quotation marks, the tag is lowercase, a comma follows, and the continuation of the spoken line is lowercase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. When a dialogue tag interrupts a single spoken sentence, both parts of the spoken line need their own quotation marks. The second part begins with a lowercase letter because it continues the same spoken sentence.

questions.text:
Stem: Which version correctly fixes the error in this sentence?

"I already told you the answer." he said with a shrug.

answers.text: "I already told you the answer". He said with a shrug.
"I already told you the answer," he said with a shrug.
I already told you the answer, he said with a shrug.
"I already told you the answer" he said, with a shrug.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The period inside the quotation marks changes to a comma so that the dialogue tag "he said with a shrug" connects to the spoken line in one sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. A dialogue tag after the spoken words requires a comma, not a period, inside the closing quotation mark. Only option (b) makes that correction and keeps the rest of the sentence intact.

questions.text:
Stem: Read this sentence:

Ms. Alvarez called from the hallway, Good morning everyone.

What is missing?

answers.text: A comma after "morning"
A period at the end of the sentence
A capital letter on "good"
Quotation marks around the spoken words "Good morning everyone."

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The spoken words need quotation marks to show that they were said aloud. Without them, the sentence blends the narrator's description with the spoken words.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The dialogue tag "Ms. Alvarez called from the hallway" introduces spoken words. Those spoken words need quotation marks around them.

questions.text: Stem: Which of the following sentences correctly uses the speaker-at-start dialogue pattern?

answers.text: Marcus asked, "Is the library still open?"
Marcus asked, "Is the library still open"?
Marcus asked "Is the library still open?"
"Marcus asked," Is the library still open?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Option (a) shows the correct speaker-at-start pattern: dialogue tag introducer, comma, opening quotation mark, spoken words, question mark inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. In the speaker-at-start pattern, a comma follows the dialogue tag introducer, and all end punctuation for the spoken words sits inside the closing quotation mark. Only option (a) follows both rules.

questions.text:
In Chapter 9, two rival groups meet for a large, organized fight that both sides have agreed to in advance. What name does the novel use for this kind of planned group confrontation?

Answers:

answers.text: a showdown
a rumble
a riot
a standoff

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The planned fight between the two groups in Chapter 9 is called a rumble. Knowing this term helps you follow the sequence of events that leads to the chapter's outcome.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Look back at Chapter 9: both groups agree ahead of time to a structured fight. The novel uses a specific word for this. Review the chapter for that term.

questions.text:
After the fight in Chapter 9, Ponyboy receives urgent news that leads him to the hospital. Which two characters is he rushing to see?

Answers:

answers.text: Sodapop and Two-Bit
Darry and Steve
Johnny and Dally
Cherry and Randy

questions.feedback_correct: Right. After the rumble, Ponyboy goes to the hospital to see Johnny and Dally. The events that follow in Chapters 9 and 10 center on what happens to both of them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. After the rumble ends in Chapter 9, the story shifts immediately. Two characters who were wounded earlier are still at the hospital. Re-read the transition between Chapters 9 and 10 to identify who Ponyboy is going to see.

questions.text:
By the end of Chapter 10, Ponyboy has experienced two major losses in close succession. What effect do those losses have on him in the final pages of the chapter?

Answers:

answers.text: He decides to leave town with his brothers.
He goes into a state of shock and denial, struggling to accept what has happened.
He becomes angry at the Socs and wants to fight again.
He writes a letter to Cherry explaining everything.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. By the end of Chapter 10, the weight of what has happened overwhelms Ponyboy and he moves into a state of shock and denial. This sets up the emotional journey that carries through the rest of the novel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Two major events hit Ponyboy in very quick succession at the end of Chapter 10. Think about how someone might react when multiple painful things happen faster than they can process them. Reread the final pages of Chapter 10.

questions.text:
A story's climax is the moment of highest tension, after which the outcome becomes clear and things begin to resolve. Which of the following best describes what a climax does in a plot?

Answers:

answers.text: It introduces the main characters and their situation.
It provides background history the reader needs to understand the story.
It wraps up loose ends after the main conflict is resolved.
It is the turning point where the conflict reaches its peak and the story's direction becomes decided.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The climax is the turning point: tension reaches its peak, and from that moment on, the story moves toward resolution rather than building toward more conflict.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The climax is not where the story begins or where it ends. It is the high point in the middle, the moment when the central conflict is most intense and the direction of the story becomes clear. Review your notes on plot structure from this week.

questions.text:
When a reader pays attention to the sequence of events in a novel, they are doing more than just tracking what happened first, second, and third. What does careful attention to sequence help a reader understand?

Answers:

answers.text: Why one event causes or shapes the next, and how the order of events creates meaning
The number of characters in each chapter
The exact words a character uses in a conversation
The physical description of the setting

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Sequence is about more than order: it is about causation and meaning. When you notice how one event leads to the next, you start to see the author's choices, not just the story's facts.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Sequence is not just a timeline of events. Think about why the order matters: what happens because of what came before it? That relationship between events is what sequence analysis is really about.

questions.text:
Throughout the novel, the greasers act as a chosen family for each other, especially for Ponyboy. Which statement best describes what the novel suggests about loyalty and family?

Answers:

answers.text: Loyalty only exists between people who are related by blood.
A family that argues frequently cannot be truly loyal to one another.
True loyalty means showing up for someone even when the cost to yourself is high.
Family bonds are less important than fitting in with a larger social group.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The novel consistently shows loyalty as something demonstrated through action under pressure, not just expressed in words. The greasers repeatedly show up for each other at real personal cost.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Think about how the greasers behave toward each other throughout the novel, especially in Chapters 9 and 10. What does loyalty actually look like in the story? It is not about words; it is about what people do when things get hard.

questions.text:
Read the following sentence. Which version is correctly punctuated?

Answers:

answers.text: "The trail ends here." Marcus said, pointing at the map.
"The trail ends here," Marcus said, pointing at the map.
"The trail ends here", Marcus said, pointing at the map.
The trail ends here, Marcus said, pointing at the map.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. When a dialogue tag follows the spoken words, use a comma inside the closing quotation mark, not a period. Option b places the comma correctly.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Review the dialogue punctuation rules from this week. When the spoken line is followed by a dialogue tag like "Marcus said," the period inside the quoted speech becomes a comma. The comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.text:
A student wrote the following sentence in a story. What is the error?

Priya whispered, "Nobody saw us leave".

Answers:

answers.text: There should be no comma after "whispered."
The word "whispered" should be capitalized.
The sentence does not need quotation marks.
The period belongs inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In American English, the period always goes inside the closing quotation mark. The corrected sentence reads: Priya whispered, "Nobody saw us leave."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Look carefully at where the period lands in the sentence. In American English, periods and commas go inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it. Review Error Type 3 from this week's grammar lesson.

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 6: Commonly Confused Words and Proofreading and Editing)

questions.text: Which sentence uses the correct word?

answers.text: Their going to present their findings tomorrow.
There going to present their findings tomorrow.
They're going to present their findings tomorrow.
Theyre going to present there findings tomorrow.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. They're is a contraction for they are. Substitute "they are" and the sentence works.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Try substituting "they are" into the blank. If that fits, use the contraction they're. Their shows ownership; there shows a place.

questions.text: Which word correctly completes this sentence? "The cold weather began to ___ his recovery."

answers.text: effect
affect
effected
affection

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Affect is the verb form meaning to influence or change. Began to affect shows an action.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The blank needs a verb (an action word). Affect is the verb. Effect is usually the noun naming the result.

questions.text: Which sentence uses its and it's correctly?

answers.text: The team celebrated it's win with their coach.
Its going to be a difficult day for the whole group.
The group had its own set of rules, and it's easy to see why.
It's own strength surprised everyone who saw it.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Its shows ownership (the group's rules). It's means it is (it is easy to see why).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Test each one: can you say "it is" in that spot? If yes, write it's. If no, write its (no apostrophe).

questions.text: Which sentence uses then and than correctly?

answers.text: He was braver then anyone expected him to be.
She finished her work, than she went outside.
The second answer was better then the first.
He worked longer than anyone else, then took a break.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Than is used for comparison (longer than); then is used for time (then took a break).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Remember: than = comparison; then = time. Try substituting "at that point" for then or "compared to" for than.

questions.text: A student wrote: "The effect of the news were immediate and obvious." What is wrong?

answers.text: Effect should be affect.
The subject noun effect is singular, so were should be was.
Immediate should be immediately.
Nothing is wrong.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The subject noun effect is singular, so the verb should be was, not were. Effect is the correct word here because it names the result (noun).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the subject noun first. Ask "who or what were?" The answer is effect. Is effect singular or plural? That tells you which verb to use.

questions.text: Which sentence has NO error?

answers.text: Their are three reasons why he made that choice.
The decision effected everyone in the group differently.
He was taller then his older brother by three inches.
The gang kept its code of loyalty no matter what.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Its is the possessive (the gang's code). No error in this sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each sentence for the confused-word pairs. Which sentence passes all four checks: their/there/they're, affect/effect, its/it's, then/than?

questions.text: A student is proofreading an essay paragraph. Which step should come first?

answers.text: Check every sentence for run-on sentences and fragments.
Read the paragraph aloud to catch awkward phrasing.
Read slowly, word by word, checking each word's spelling.
Rewrite the entire introduction.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The first pass is a slow, word-by-word spelling check. The other steps follow after.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Proofreading works in passes. The first pass is the most careful: read word by word for spelling, before checking grammar or reading aloud.

questions.text: A student wrote: "Him and his brother walked to school every morning." What is wrong?

answers.text: Every should be each.
Walked should be walk.
Him should be He because the word is the subject of the sentence.
Nothing is wrong.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The subject pronoun in a sentence is He, she, they, we, or I, not Him. Ask "who or what walked?" The answer is He and his brother.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the subject pronoun: ask "who or what walked?" Object pronouns like him, her, them cannot be the subject of a sentence.

questions.text: In Chapter 11, a character visits Ponyboy at home to talk about what happened. Who is that visitor?

answers.text: Cherry Valance
Randy
Two-Bit
Darry

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Randy visits Ponyboy in Chapter 11 and they have an honest conversation about what both of them are feeling.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look back at the beginning of Chapter 11. Think about who would want to talk to Ponyboy at this point in the story.

questions.text: The term "frame narrative" describes:

answers.text: A story told using a series of diary entries.
A story told entirely from multiple points of view.
A story in which the act of telling the story is itself part of the plot.
A story with no clear ending.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In a frame narrative, the outer frame is someone in the act of telling or writing a story. The events are the inner story.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about how the frame-and-narrator lesson described the outer frame of this novel. What does Ponyboy decide to do by the end of Chapter 12, and how does that connect to the first sentence of the book?

questions.text: By the end of Chapter 12, Ponyboy decides to:

answers.text: Move to a new city and start over.
Drop out of school.
Write down everything that happened.
Become a lawyer.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ponyboy decides to write his school theme about what happened. That decision is the hinge of the novel's frame.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the very end of Chapter 12. What does Ponyboy choose to do, and how does it connect to the novel's first chapter?

questions.text: Which sentence uses the correct word?

answers.text: The news began to effect everyone in the house.
The news began to affect everyone in the house.
The effect of the news begun to settle in.
The affect was felt by everyone who heard it.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Affect is the verb meaning to influence or change. "Began to affect" shows an action.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The blank follows a helping verb (began to), so you need the verb form. Affect is the verb; effect is usually the noun.

questions.text: Which sentence uses then and than correctly?

answers.text: She was calmer then he was, and then she spoke.
He was calmer than she was, and then he spoke.
He was calmer then she was, and than he spoke.
She was calmer than he was, and than she spoke.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Than shows comparison (calmer than). Then shows time (then he spoke).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Remember: than = comparison; then = time. Both words appear in the correct answer, each doing its own job.

questions.text: A student wrote: "There going to finish the project before the deadline." What is wrong?

answers.text: Finish should be finishing.
Before should be by.
There should be They're (they are).
Nothing is wrong.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. They're means they are. Substitute "they are going" and it works. There refers to a place, not a subject.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Try substituting "they are" into the first word. If that fits, use the contraction they're.

questions.text: Which word from Chapter 11-12 means "accepting something difficult without fighting it"?

answers.text: contemptuously
imploring
bewildered
resigned

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Resigned describes a state of quiet acceptance when you stop fighting something you cannot change.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review your Word Study for this week. Think about which word describes the emotional state of giving in or accepting without protest.

questions.text: Which is the correct first step in proofreading a paragraph?

answers.text: Rewrite the whole introduction.
Read the paragraph aloud to catch awkward phrasing.
Read slowly, word by word, checking each word's spelling.
Ask a classmate to check it first.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The first proofreading pass is the careful word-by-word spelling check. The other steps follow after that.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Proofreading works in passes. The first pass is the most careful: read word by word before moving on to grammar or reading aloud.

quizzes.title: Module 4 Outro: The Outsiders
quizzes.description: This survey looks back on Module 4. Honest answers show the teacher what landed and what to revisit.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your refined answer. Look back at how you answered this in the Module Intro: **What divides the greasers and the Socs, and what does the novel say stays the same on both sides?

Answer it again now, in three or four sentences, using something specific from the novel (for example, what Ponyboy learns about a Soc character, the meaning of "staying gold," or the way the gang treats one another like family). How has your answer changed since the start?

(Survey, no scoring. Compare to the Q1 intro response to see growth.)
Confidence rating. How confident do you feel that you can explain a theme from The Outsiders and back it up with evidence from the novel?

answers.text: Very confident
Mostly confident
Somewhat confident
Not yet confident

questions.text:
What still feels unclear. Name one thing about The Outsiders, its themes, or the literary-analysis writing skills in this module that still feels unclear or that you would like more practice with. If everything feels clear, say what you found hardest.

(Survey, free response. Teachers scan for common confusion points.)

Virtue reflection. Optima names seven virtues: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. This module is about loyalty, family, and holding on to something good in hard circumstances. Pick the ONE virtue the novel most asked of its characters, and that this module asked of you:

answers.text: Service (giving of yourself for the people who depend on you, even at personal cost)
Courage (choosing what is right when it is dangerous or costly)
Honesty (seeing yourself and others clearly, without the lens of your group)
Another of the seven virtues

quizzes.title: Module 4B Intro: A Midsummer Night's Dream
quizzes.description: Module 4B covers A Midsummer Night's Dream by William Shakespeare, a play about four young lovers, a pair of quarreling fairy rulers, and a group of amateur actors, all of whom spend one strange night in a wood outside Athens. Almost everyone in this play ends up telling a story about what happened that night, and the stories do not all agree. The play is read as dialogue and stage directions rather than narration. The full text is provided in each lesson; no outside copy is needed.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your first answer. Our question for this whole module is: **Everyone in this play tells a story about what happened in the wood. Whose account can we trust, and how would we know?

In two or three sentences, give your first answer. Before reading the play, state an expectation: when two people tell different stories about the same event, how is the decision about who to believe usually made?

(Survey, no scoring. Used to compare against the Q1 response on the module outro.)

Module objectives: check each box to show you have read it. By the end of this module, the student will be able to:

- [ ] Read all nine scenes of A Midsummer Night's Dream and follow the major events of the plot. - [ ] Explain how a play works: dialogue, stage directions, and the difference between verse and prose. - [ ] Notice how blank verse, rhymed couplets, and prose each shape how a scene sounds and feels. - [ ] Track how several characters narrate the same night differently, and compare their accounts to what the audience actually saw happen. - [ ] Recognize classical allusions the play makes (to figures such as Cupid and Diana) and explain what they add to a scene. - [ ] Write a literary-analysis essay: a claim about whose account deserves belief, supported by evidence cited in MLA format (Shakespeare's name plus act.scene), with a Works Cited entry for the play.

(Survey item. Acknowledgment, not a right answer; all boxes are correct to check.)
Group work opt-in. The final project can be done on your own or with one partner. Both paths get the same instructions and the same kind of feedback. Which do you want for this module?

answers.text: I will work on my own.
I would like to work with a partner (your teacher will help arrange this).
I am not sure yet; I will decide before the project opens.

questions.text:
One thing you are curious about. Name one thing about fairies, love, mistaken identity, or this play that you are curious to find out. One sentence is fine.

(Survey, no scoring. Light engagement signal.)

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 1: Verb Tenses and Semicolons, Colons, and Dashes)

questions.text: "The court gathers here every morning." What tense is the verb gathers?

answers.text: past
present
future
past perfect

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Gathers shows something that happens regularly now, so it is present tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: If something is happening now or is always true, the verb is in the present tense. Look at when the action takes place.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the PAST tense correctly?

answers.text: She will explain her plan tomorrow.
They are leaving the city tonight.
He remembered every word of the ruling.
The door opens slowly.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Remembered shows an action that already happened, so it is past tense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the verb that shows something already completed or finished.

questions.text: "By the time the Duke arrived, the argument had already begun." The verb phrase had begun is an example of:

answers.text: future tense
present tense
future perfect
past perfect

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Past perfect uses had plus a main verb. It shows one past event was already completed before another past event.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When had comes before a main verb, it creates the past perfect: something was already done when something else happened in the past.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a SEMICOLON?

answers.text: She argued; because she believed she was right.
He raised his hand; the room went quiet.
The list included; songs, tokens, and letters.
She wanted; to be heard.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both parts are complete sentences, so a semicolon correctly joins them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A semicolon joins two complete, independent sentences. Check that each side can stand on its own.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a COLON?

answers.text: She needed: more time to decide.
The teacher explained: the rule carefully.
There are three choices: obey, marry, or refuse.
He ran: as fast as he could.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The colon follows a complete statement and introduces the list that explains it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon works after a complete sentence when a list or explanation follows immediately.

questions.text: "He had only one hope, one plan, one chance: to be believed." What does the colon do in this sentence?

answers.text: Joins two complete sentences.
Introduces the explanation of what his hope, plan, and chance were.
Shows that a list of verbs is coming.
Replaces a question mark.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The colon points to the answer for what the hope, plan, and chance were.
questions.feedback_incorrect: What comes after the colon? It names the one thing the sentence has been building toward.

questions.text: A sentence uses had before a main verb: "She had finished her plan before nightfall." What is had doing?

answers.text: It is a linking verb showing a state of being.
It is an adverb.
It is the subject noun.
It is a helping verb that forms the past perfect.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Had plus the main verb finished creates the past perfect. The helping verb shows the action was already completed before another past event.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When had comes before a main verb in the past tense, it is a helping verb forming the past perfect.

questions.text: Which mark belongs in the blank? "She made one request __ she wanted the truth told plainly."

answers.text: a comma
a colon (:)
a semicolon (;)
a period followed by a capital letter

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both parts are complete, independent sentences, and they are closely related, so a semicolon joins them well.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Both parts are complete sentences. A semicolon specifically joins two closely related independent clauses.

quizzes.title: Check-up: Week 1 (Module 4B: A Midsummer Night's Dream)

questions.text: In a play script, bracketed text describing the setting or telling actors what to do is called:

answers.text: a speaker label
a stage direction
a soliloquy
a stanza

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A stage direction tells actors and stage crew what to do; it is never spoken aloud.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for text that instructs the actors or describes the scene rather than being spoken by a character.

questions.text: In Act 1, which characters in the play tend to speak in prose rather than verse?

answers.text: Theseus and Hippolyta
The fairies
Quince, Bottom, and the other craftsmen
Egeus and the Duke

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The craftsmen preparing their own play speak in ordinary prose, while the nobles at court speak in verse.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about which group is working-class and speaking casually to one another, rather than addressing the Duke formally.

questions.text: What is Egeus's claim in his complaint to Theseus?

answers.text: That Demetrius has broken the law.
That Hermia has already agreed to marry Lysander.
That, as her father, he has the right to decide who Hermia marries.
That Lysander should be exiled from Athens.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Egeus claims a father's right to dispose of his daughter's marriage as he sees fit.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the core belief Egeus wants Theseus to accept, not the specific details he uses to support it.

questions.text: Which of the following is evidence Egeus offers to support his complaint?

answers.text: Demetrius's promise to marry Hermia
Lysander's gifts, songs, and love-tokens given to Hermia
A letter written by Hermia herself
A ruling from an earlier court case

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Egeus lists specific courtship gifts and actions as proof of what he calls bewitchment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Egeus lists specific things Lysander did. What details does he actually name?

questions.text: What does Egeus demand from Theseus?

answers.text: That Hermia be forgiven and allowed to choose freely.
That Lysander be forced to apologize.
That Hermia marry Demetrius or face death or a vow of celibacy, under Athenian law.
That the wedding between Theseus and Hippolyta be postponed.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Egeus invokes the ancient privilege of Athens and demands that ruling be enforced.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Egeus names a specific law and a specific outcome he wants enforced. What is it?

questions.text: "She had already accepted the plan before her friend arrived." What tense is the verb phrase had accepted?

answers.text: Present tense
Future perfect
Simple past
Past perfect

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Past perfect uses "had" plus a main verb. It shows one past action was already completed before another past action happened.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When "had" comes before a main verb, it creates a special past form. What tense shows that one past event was already done when another past event occurred?

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a COLON?

answers.text: She ran: because she was late.
He called: his closest friend immediately.
The plan required three things: courage, timing, and silence.
They left: before the ruling was given.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The colon follows a complete sentence and introduces the list that explains the three things.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A colon introduces a list or explanation. It must follow a complete sentence. Which option has a complete statement before the colon AND a true list after it?

questions.text: Why does Lysander want to reach his aunt's house outside Athens?

answers.text: She has agreed to speak to Egeus on his behalf.
Athenian law cannot follow them there.
Demetrius does not know the way there.
The Duke has ordered them to go there.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Lysander explains that his aunt's house is beyond the reach of the sharp Athenian law.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the specific reason Lysander gives for choosing this particular destination.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a SEMICOLON?

answers.text: She left quietly; because no one noticed.
He wanted three things; loyalty, patience, and time.
The plan was risky; she agreed to it anyway.
The door opened; a cold wind swept through the room, and everyone turned around, startled by the sudden gust.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both parts are complete, closely related sentences. A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A semicolon joins two complete, independent sentences. Check each option: can both sides stand alone as complete sentences, and are they closely related?

questions.text: After learning about Hermia and Lysander's plan, what does Helena decide to do?

answers.text: Keep the secret to protect her friend.
Warn Egeus immediately.
Tell Demetrius, hoping it will win her some of his gratitude.
Follow the couple into the wood without telling anyone.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Helena decides to tell Demetrius the secret, even though she suspects it will cost her more than it gains her.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about who Helena loves and what she hopes telling him the secret will accomplish.

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz: Parts of Speech Review and Active and Passive Voice (Week 2)

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

Which word is the subject noun in this sentence?

"The mischievous sprite hid behind an old oak."

answers.text: mischievous
sprite
hid
oak

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Sprite is the noun that performs the action. It answers "who or what hid?" so sprite is the subject noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb hid, then ask "who or what hid?" The noun that answers that question is the subject noun.

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

In this sentence, which word is an adverb?

"She carefully placed the flower on the sleeping man's eyelids."

answers.text: carefully
sleeping
flower
placed

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Carefully tells how she placed the flower. It answers "placed how?" so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb placed and ask "placed how?" The word that answers that question is the adverb.

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

The words a, an, and the belong to which category?

answers.text: pronouns
prepositions
article adjectives
interjections

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A, an, and the are article adjectives. They point to a noun and answer "which one."
questions.feedback_incorrect: A, an, and the always point to a noun. That makes them article adjectives.

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

In this sentence, which word is a conjunction?

"Titania and her fairies danced in the moonlit grove."

answers.text: moonlit
danced
and
grove

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. And joins "Titania" and "her fairies." Connecting two parts of a sentence is a conjunction's job.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that connects two parts of the sentence. That connecting word is a conjunction.

questions.text:
Parts of Speech

What question do you ask to find the subject in any sentence?

answers.text: What kind? Which one? How many?
How? When? Where? To what extent?
Who or what [verb]?
What is the action being received?

questions.feedback_correct: Right. To find the subject, find the verb first and then ask "who or what [verb]?" The noun or pronoun that answers is the subject.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The subject-finding question is "who or what [verb]?" using the verb you already found in the sentence.

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

Which sentence is in active voice?

answers.text: The wrong man was anointed with the flower's juice.
A mistake had been made in the darkness.
Puck anointed the wrong man with the flower's juice.
The quarrel was blamed for the ruined harvest.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Puck (subject) is performing the action of anointing. When the subject acts, the sentence is in active voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In active voice the subject performs the action. Which sentence has the subject doing something rather than having something done to it?

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

In a passive-voice sentence, the verb usually includes:

answers.text: an action verb with no helping verb
a helping verb paired with a past-participle main verb
two action verbs in a row
an article adjective before the verb

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Passive voice combines a helping verb (was, were, is, are, has been, etc.) with a past-participle main verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the combination of a helping verb plus a past-participle main verb. That pattern is the signal for passive voice.

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

Which sentence is in passive voice?

answers.text: The fairy king demanded the changeling boy.
Titania refused to give up the boy.
The wood confused the two Athenian couples.
The lovers' quarrel was overheard by Oberon.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The quarrel (subject) did not do any overhearing. It was acted upon. "Was overheard" is a helping verb plus past-participle main verb, so this is passive voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask whether the subject is doing the action or receiving it. "Was overheard by Oberon" puts the quarrel as the receiver, not the doer.

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

You want to emphasize what happened rather than who did it. Which voice is usually the better choice?

answers.text: Passive voice
Active voice
Both work equally in all situations.
Neither. You should use a question instead.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Passive voice shifts attention to the action or the result. That is useful when the doer is unknown or less important than what happened.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about which voice hides the doer and puts the spotlight on what happened.

questions.text:
Active and Passive Voice

Change this passive sentence to active voice:

"The flower was fetched by Puck."

Which version is the correct active-voice rewrite?

answers.text: The flower fetched Puck.
Puck was fetching the flower.
The flower had been fetched.
Puck fetched the flower.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Moving the doer (Puck) to the subject position and using the simple past action verb (fetched) converts the sentence to active voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In active voice the doer becomes the subject and performs the action directly. Who fetched the flower? Make that the subject.

quizzes.title: Check-up: Week 2 (A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 2)

questions.text: Compared to Athens, how is the wood in Act 2 best described?

answers.text: A place with a stricter version of Athenian law.
A place governed by night, magic, and confusion rather than a named law.
A place identical to Athens in every way.
A place no character enters during the play.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The wood replaces daylight and law with night, fairy rule, and confusion, and that change in setting is already shaping how characters behave.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread this week's opening lesson. What replaces law and daylight once the characters enter the wood?

questions.text: Why does Titania tell the story of the changeling boy's mother?

answers.text: To prove that Oberon has no right to speak to her at all.
To make her refusal to give up the boy feel justified by loyalty and memory.
To explain why she wants to leave fairyland forever.
To apologize to Oberon for the quarrel.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The tender, specific memory makes her refusal feel like loyalty rather than stubbornness.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what a warm, detailed memory does to a request to give something up. What is Titania trying to accomplish?

questions.text: What does Titania's speech about the disordered seasons ask the audience to consider?

answers.text: Whether her claim is a real cause in the play's world, a persuasive story about cause, or both.
Whether Oberon has ever visited Athens.
Whether Titania actually likes the changeling boy.
Whether the play takes place in winter.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Because fairies in this play do have power over nature, her claim could be literally true and still be a persuasive story that shifts blame onto Oberon.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the "Think About It" box in the lesson on Oberon and Titania's quarrel. The lesson holds both possibilities at once.

questions.text: Why does Puck anoint the wrong Athenian man with the flower's juice?

answers.text: Oberon secretly told him to make a mistake.
It is dark, and Puck finds a sleeping Athenian man who matches the little he was told.
Puck cannot see any difference between fairies and humans.
Lysander asked Puck to enchant him.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The wood's darkness removes the visual details that would normally prevent this mix-up, so an honest mistake follows directly from the setting.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the lesson on the love-juice and the first mistake. What feature of the wood makes it hard for Puck to tell two sleeping Athenians apart?

questions.text: What is dramatic irony?

answers.text: When a character makes a joke that nobody in the play finds funny.
When the audience knows something an onstage character does not.
When two characters argue about the same event.
When a play ends differently than the audience expects.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The audience watching Lysander wake and declare love for Helena knows exactly why: the flower. Helena and Lysander do not know that.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what you, the reader, know about the flower that Helena and Lysander do not know yet. That gap is dramatic irony.

questions.text: Which word is the adverb in "The startled sprite darted swiftly between the trees"?

answers.text: startled
darted
swiftly
between

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Swiftly" tells how the sprite darted. It answers "how" about the verb, so it is an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the verb "darted" and ask "darted how?" The word that answers that question is the adverb.

questions.text: Which sentence is in passive voice?

answers.text: Oberon sent Puck to fetch the flower.
The flower's juice was placed on the sleeper's eyes by Puck.
Titania led her fairies through the wood.
A jealous king quarreled with his queen.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Was placed" is a helping verb plus a past-participle main verb, and the subject (the juice) is receiving the action, not performing it. That is passive voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In passive voice the subject receives the action. Look for a helping verb before the main verb. Which sentence fits that pattern?

questions.text: So far in the play, whose account of events in the wood should a careful reader question most closely, and why?

answers.text: No account should ever be questioned; every character tells the truth.
A character's account is worth questioning when the character telling it has something to gain from how the listener judges it.
Only characters who are asleep can be trusted.
Only the audience's own eyes matter; no character's words matter at all.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Egeus in Week 1 and Titania this week both tell accounts shaped by what they want a listener to believe. Noticing that motive is how a reader judges whether to trust an account.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think back to Egeus's speech in Week 1 and Titania's two narrations this week. What do all of these accounts have in common?

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz: Week 3 (Sentence Structure and Adding Detail)

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "The workmen rehearsed their play in the wood."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Fragment

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. One subject (workmen), one verb (rehearsed), one independent clause. That is a simple sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Count the clauses. Is there more than one subject and verb here?

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "Puck placed a donkey's head on Bottom, and the workmen fled in terror."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Run-on

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two independent clauses joined by "and": "Puck placed a donkey's head on Bottom" and "the workmen fled in terror." Both can stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the conjunction joining the two halves. Can each half stand alone as its own sentence?

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "Because Titania was enchanted, she fell in love with Bottom."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Run-on

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Because Titania was enchanted" is a dependent clause; it starts with the subordinating conjunction "because" and cannot stand alone. "She fell in love with Bottom" is the independent clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Can "Because Titania was enchanted" stand alone as a complete sentence? A clause that cannot stand alone and starts with a word like "because" is a dependent clause.

questions.text: In "The frightened workman dropped his script," what part of speech is "frightened"?

answers.text: Adverb
Preposition
Adjective
Noun

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Frightened" answers "what kind of workman?" That is the test for an adjective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "what kind of workman?" The word that answers that question is an adjective, not an adverb or preposition.

questions.text: In "Titania woke suddenly," what part of speech is "suddenly"?

answers.text: Adjective
Adverb
Preposition
Noun

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Suddenly" answers "how did she wake?" That is the test for an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "how did she wake?" The word that answers that question is an adverb.

questions.text: In "They rehearsed under the hawthorn brake," which words form the prepositional phrase?

answers.text: They rehearsed
hawthorn brake
under the hawthorn brake
rehearsed under

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Under" is the preposition, and "brake" is the object of the preposition. The whole phrase answers "where did they rehearse?"
questions.feedback_incorrect: A prepositional phrase begins with the preposition itself. Find the word that starts the phrase and answers "where?"

questions.text: A student wrote: "Although Bottom seemed unafraid." Can this stand alone as a complete sentence?

answers.text: Yes, because it has a subject and a verb
No, because it is a dependent clause that needs an independent clause to complete it
Yes, if you add a period
No, because it has no subject

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Although" makes this a dependent clause. It needs an independent clause to complete the thought, for example: "Although Bottom seemed unafraid, his friends were terrified."
questions.feedback_incorrect: It does have a subject ("Bottom") and a verb ("seemed"), but the word "although" leaves the thought incomplete. It needs an independent clause to finish it.

quizzes.title: Check-up: Week 3 (A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 3)

questions.text: What trick does Puck play on Bottom while he is rehearsing?

answers.text: He steals Bottom's costume.
He gives Bottom the head of a donkey.
He hides Bottom's script.
He turns Bottom invisible.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Puck fixes an ass's head onto Bottom while he is out of sight of his friends.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the start of Act 3, Scene 1. Puck changes something about Bottom's appearance.

questions.text: Why does Titania fall in love with Bottom?

answers.text: She has always secretly admired him.
He performs a heroic act to save her.
She is under the enchantment of the flower's juice.
Oberon orders her to.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Oberon put the flower's juice on Titania's eyes earlier, making her fall for the first creature she sees upon waking, which is now Bottom.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think back to what Oberon did to Titania while she slept. Her sudden love is a magical effect, not a real choice.

questions.text: A passage keeps a steady five-beat rhythm across every line but never rhymes. What form is this?

answers.text: Prose
Rhymed couplets
Blank verse
A stage direction

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A steady beat with no rhyme is blank verse.
questions.feedback_incorrect: If the lines do not rhyme but still keep a steady beat, that combination has a specific name: blank verse.

questions.text: Which group of characters in this play speaks in ordinary prose, with no set beat and no rhyme?

answers.text: The fairies
The workmen (the mechanicals)
Theseus and Hippolyta
Oberon and Titania

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The workmen, Bottom, Quince, Snout, and the others, speak in plain prose, which fits their lower status and adds to the comedy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about which characters are treated as lower-status and more comic in the play. Their speech has no beat and no rhyme.

questions.text: Helena compares her childhood friendship with Hermia to a "double cherry" and "two lovely berries." What is she arguing by using that image?

answers.text: That she and Hermia used to look alike.
That she and Hermia grew from one shared bond and should not be truly separated.
That she misses eating fruit with Hermia.
That fruit trees grow well in Athens.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The image shows two things that look separate but come from one source, which is Helena's argument for why Hermia should not have turned on her.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what a cherry with two halves on one stem represents about closeness and shared origin.

questions.text: Why does Helena tell this childhood story in the middle of an argument?

answers.text: She is trying to change the subject.
She wants to use the shared past as evidence that Hermia's betrayal does not make sense.
Quince asked everyone to share a memory.
She has confused Hermia with someone else.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Helena uses the narrated past as evidence in her present argument, the same move other characters make elsewhere in the play.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what Helena wants Hermia to do because of the story. She is not just remembering for its own sake.

questions.text:
Read this sentence: "Because Puck tricked him, Bottom's friends fled."

What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Complex
Fragment

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Because Puck tricked him" is a dependent clause; it cannot stand alone and starts with the subordinating conjunction "because." "Bottom's friends fled" is the independent clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Can "Because Puck tricked him" stand alone as a full sentence? A clause that cannot and starts with a word like "because" is dependent, which makes the sentence complex.

questions.text: In "Titania woke suddenly," what part of speech is "suddenly"?

answers.text: Adjective
Preposition
Noun
Adverb, because it answers "how?" about the verb

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Suddenly" answers "how did she wake?" That is the test for an adverb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "how did she wake?" The word that answers that question describes the verb, which makes it an adverb.

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 4: Capitalization and Punctuation + Punctuating Titles and Quotations)

questions.text:
Which word in this sentence needs to be capitalized?

"Every wednesday, the fairies gather in the wood."

answers.text: every
fairies
wednesday
wood

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Wednesday is the name of a specific day of the week, so it is a proper noun and must be capitalized.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the word that names a specific day, month, or proper noun. Days of the week are always capitalized.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly capitalizes the title used before a name?

answers.text: She spoke with duke Theseus about the wedding.
She spoke with Duke Theseus about the wedding.
She Spoke With duke Theseus About The Wedding.
she spoke with duke theseus about the wedding.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A title used directly before a person's name is capitalized: Duke Theseus.
questions.feedback_incorrect: When a title comes right before a specific person's name, it is capitalized. When it stands alone, it is lowercase.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the correct end mark?

answers.text: Did Puck sprinkle the wrong sleeper's eyes.
Did Puck sprinkle the wrong sleeper's eyes?
Did Puck sprinkle the wrong sleeper's eyes!
Did Puck sprinkle the wrong sleeper's eyes;

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The sentence asks a question, so it ends with a question mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the purpose of the sentence. A sentence that asks something is interrogative and ends with a question mark.

questions.text:
Which word in this sentence should NOT be capitalized?

"Two Fairies from athens waited near Titania's bower."

answers.text: Fairies
athens (needs to be capitalized)
Titania
bower

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Fairies is a common noun; it should not be capitalized in the middle of a sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Athens and Titania are proper nouns and must be capitalized. Fairies is a common noun used in the middle of a sentence: no capital letter needed.

questions.text: Which sentence uses title punctuation correctly for a play?

answers.text: He had seen "A Midsummer Night's Dream" twice.
He had seen A MIDSUMMER NIGHT'S DREAM twice.
He had seen A Midsummer Night's Dream twice.
He had seen A Midsummer Night's Dream twice.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A full-length play is a long work, so its title is italicized (or underlined in handwriting).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Long works like plays get italics (or underlining in handwriting). Quotation marks are for short works like poems and ballads.

questions.text: Which sentence uses title punctuation correctly for a ballad?

answers.text: Quince agreed to write Bottom's Dream for him.
Quince agreed to write Bottom's Dream for him.
Quince agreed to write "Bottom's Dream" for him.
Quince agreed to write BOTTOM'S DREAM for him.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A ballad is a short work, so its title goes in quotation marks.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Short works like ballads, poems, and short stories go in quotation marks. Italics are for long works like full-length plays and novels.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly introduces a quotation with a signal phrase?

answers.text: Bottom announced "I have had a most rare vision."
Bottom announced, "I have had a most rare vision."
Bottom announced. "I have had a most rare vision."
Bottom announced "I have had a most rare vision," it was true.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A comma follows the signal phrase before the opening quotation mark. The period goes inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A signal phrase is followed by a comma, then the opening quotation mark. The period belongs inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.text: Where does the period go when a sentence ends with a quoted passage (and no citation follows it)?

answers.text: After the closing quotation mark, outside it.
Before the opening quotation mark.
Inside the closing quotation mark.
There is no period; the quotation mark ends the sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In American English, the period goes inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In American English, periods and commas always go inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is a proper noun? "The duke announced the wedding date in June."

answers.text: duke
wedding
date
June

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. June names a specific month, so it is a proper noun and is capitalized. Duke is lowercase here because it is used alone, not directly before a name.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A proper noun names a specific person, place, day, or month. Look for the word that names a specific month.

questions.text: A sentence that gives a strong command ends with:

answers.text: A comma
A question mark
A semicolon
A period or an exclamation mark

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Imperative sentences (commands or requests) typically end with a period; when the command is urgent or emotional, an exclamation mark is correct.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A command is an imperative sentence. It ends with a period for a calm instruction or an exclamation mark for a forceful or urgent one.

quizzes.title: Check-up: Week 4 (A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 4)

questions.text: After Oberon undoes the spell, what does Titania say about her time with Bottom?

answers.text: She says it was the best night of her life.
She says, "Methought I was enamour'd of an ass," and is confused and a little disgusted.
She says she remembers nothing at all happened.
She demands Bottom be punished.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Titania wakes confused and put off once the spell lifts; the play treats this moment as comedy, not romance.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look again at Titania's own reaction right after Oberon releases her. Is she pleased, or startled?

questions.text: What does Lysander tell Duke Theseus about how he ended up asleep in the wood with Hermia?

answers.text: He gives a confident, carefully planned account.
He is honestly unsure. He admits he can barely explain how he came there.
He blames Egeus for the whole situation.
He says Puck told him to go there.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Lysander says he will "reply amazedly," half asleep and half awake, and is not fully sure how he got there.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about how certain Lysander actually sounds when the Duke questions him.

questions.text: What happens to Demetrius's love for Hermia by the end of Act 4, Scene 1?

answers.text: It grows even stronger than before.
It disappears, and his earlier love for Helena returns and feels permanent.
It stays exactly the same as it was.
He decides he loves neither of them.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Demetrius says his love for Hermia "melted as the snow," and his love for Helena has returned.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Demetrius's speech to the Duke. Whose name does he end up choosing?

questions.text: Why can't Bottom describe his dream to his friends?

answers.text: He has completely forgotten it.
He insists that ordinary senses and words cannot capture something this strange.
He is too embarrassed to say anything.
His friends refuse to listen to him.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Bottom insists eye, ear, hand, tongue, and heart cannot hold or report what happened to him.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at what Bottom actually says about his own dream. Does he say he forgot, or something else?

questions.text: What does Bottom decide to do about his dream instead of describing it directly?

answers.text: Keep it a permanent secret.
Write a full account himself in a letter.
Ask Peter Quince to turn it into a ballad called "Bottom's Dream."
Ask Titania to explain it to everyone.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Bottom plans to have Peter Quince write a ballad and perform it at the end of their play.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at the very end of Bottom's speech for the plan he makes.

questions.text: Which sentence uses title punctuation correctly?

answers.text: Quince agreed to write "Bottom's Dream" for him, to be sung inside A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Quince agreed to write Bottom's Dream for him, to be sung inside A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Quince agreed to write Bottom's Dream for him, to be sung inside "A Midsummer Night's Dream."
Quince agreed to write BOTTOM'S DREAM for him, to be sung inside A MIDSUMMER NIGHT'S DREAM.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The ballad (a short work) gets quotation marks; the full-length play (a long work) gets italics.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Short works like a ballad get quotation marks. Long works like a full-length play get italics.

questions.text: Which correctly formats an in-text citation for a line from a play?

answers.text: (page 128)
(Shakespeare, 4.1)
(Shakespeare, page 128)

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Our pages have no page numbers, so a play is cited by the playwright's name plus act and scene, separated by a period, not by a page number.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complete citation needs both the playwright's name and the act and scene, for example (Shakespeare, 4.1).

questions.text: Which word in this sentence should be capitalized? "The wedding feast will begin in athens after the ceremony."

answers.text: wedding
feast
athens
ceremony

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Athens names a specific city, so it is a proper noun and must be capitalized.
