questions.feedback_incorrect: A proper noun names a specific person, place, or thing. Look for the word that names a specific city.

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 5: Dialogue Punctuation and Correcting Dialogue)

questions.text:
Stem: Read the sentence below. Where does the comma belong?

"The lion is not real" Snug explained.

Which version places the comma correctly?

answers.text: "The lion is not real," Snug explained.
"The lion is not real" Snug, explained.
"The lion is not real", Snug explained.
,"The lion is not real" Snug explained.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, directly after the last word of the spoken line, before the dialogue tag.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. When a dialogue tag follows the spoken words, the comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark. Look again at option (a).

questions.text:
Stem: A student wrote this sentence:

Theseus announced, "We will hear that play."

Which statement correctly describes the punctuation in this sentence?

answers.text: The comma is in the wrong place; it should come after the quotation mark.
The period should be outside the quotation mark.
The sentence is correctly punctuated: comma after the tag, spoken words in quotation marks, period inside the closing quotation mark.
The spoken words do not need quotation marks because a dialogue tag is already present.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. This is a speaker-at-the-start pattern. The comma follows the tag, the spoken words sit inside quotation marks, and the period sits inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Read the sentence again. The comma follows the tag correctly, the spoken words are inside quotation marks, and the period is inside the closing quotation mark. That is the correct form for this pattern.

questions.text: Stem: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

answers.text: "Well moused" Theseus said.
"Well moused," Theseus said.
"Well moused", Theseus said.
"Well moused." Theseus said.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. The comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark when a dialogue tag follows. Option (b) places it exactly right.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. When spoken words come first and a dialogue tag follows, the period at the end of the spoken line changes to a comma, and that comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark.

questions.text:
Stem: Read this sentence:

Hippolyta whispered, "I pity the man".

What is the error?

answers.text: The comma after "whispered" should not be there.
The period is outside the closing quotation mark; it should be inside.
The spoken words do not need quotation marks.
"whispered" should be capitalized.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In American English, the period always goes inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Look at where the period lands. In American English, a period at the end of a quoted sentence belongs inside the closing quotation mark, not after it.

questions.text:
Stem: A student wrote this sentence:

"I think," Bottom said "the lion should roar louder."

What is missing?

answers.text: A comma after "said," before the second opening quotation mark.
A capital letter to start the word "the."
Quotation marks around the word "said."
Nothing; the sentence is correct as written.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In the interrupted pattern, a comma follows the dialogue tag, before the second half of the dialogue begins.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Look at what comes right after the word "said." In the interrupted pattern, a comma separates the tag from the second half of the dialogue.

questions.text: Stem: Which sentence correctly uses the interrupted (speaker-in-the-middle) pattern?

answers.text: "I fear," Pyramus said "my Thisbe's promise is forgot."
"I fear, Pyramus said, my Thisbe's promise is forgot."
"I fear," Pyramus said, "my Thisbe's promise is forgot."
"I fear," Pyramus, said "my Thisbe's promise is forgot."

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Both halves of the dialogue have their own quotation marks, a comma closes the first half inside the quote, and a comma follows the tag.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Check each half of the dialogue for its own quotation marks, and check that a comma, not a missing mark, separates the tag from the second half.

questions.text:
Stem: Read the sentence below. What is the error?

Snout explained "This wall has a chink in it."

answers.text: A comma is missing after "explained," before the quotation mark.
The period should be outside the closing quotation mark.
"Snout" should not be capitalized.
There is no error.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. When the tag comes first, a comma separates it from the opening quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Look at what comes between "explained" and the opening quotation mark. A comma belongs there.

questions.text: Stem: Which sentence needs no correction?

answers.text: "The wall is down between the two neighbours," Theseus said.
"The wall is down between the two neighbours" Theseus said.
"The wall is down between the two neighbours", Theseus said.
"The wall is down between the two neighbours." Theseus, said.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The comma sits inside the closing quotation mark, and the tag follows correctly with a period at the end.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Compare each option to the speaker-at-the-end pattern: comma inside the closing quote, then the tag, then a period.

quizzes.title: Check-up: Week 5 (A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 5 Scene 1)

questions.text:
When Theseus hears the lovers' account of the night in the wood, what is his reaction?

Answers:

answers.text: He believes every detail immediately.
He doubts it, comparing it to the inventions of lunatics, lovers, and poets.
He refuses to let the lovers speak about it at all.
He asks Philostrate to investigate what really happened.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Theseus dismisses the account, arguing that strong imagination, not fact, produced the lovers' story.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Reread Theseus's opening speech in Act 5, Scene 1. He compares the lovers to lunatics and poets, all people whose imagination he says cannot be trusted.

questions.text:
What is Hippolyta's response to Theseus?

Answers:

answers.text: She agrees completely and dismisses the lovers' story as well.
She refuses to discuss it and changes the subject.
She points out that all four lovers' accounts agree in strange, specific ways, which she says is more than fancy.
She says only Hermia's account can be trusted.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Hippolyta argues that the story "grows to something of great constancy" because it holds together across four separate tellers.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Look again at Hippolyta's short reply right after Theseus finishes speaking. She does not dismiss the story; she offers a reason to take it seriously.

questions.text:
What entertainment does Theseus finally choose for the evening, after reviewing several options?

Answers:

answers.text: The battle with the Centaurs.
The riot of the tipsy Bacchanals.
The nine Muses mourning for learning.
"A tedious brief scene of young Pyramus and his love Thisbe."

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Despite Philostrate warning him the play is badly performed, Theseus chooses to hear it anyway.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Reread Philostrate's list of options and Theseus's response. He chooses the one description that Philostrate warns him against.

questions.text:
What are Theseus and Hippolyta actually disagreeing about?

Answers:

answers.text: What specific events happened in the wood.
How much an account deserves to be believed, and what should count as evidence.
Whether the lovers should be punished.
Which lover is telling the truth and which is lying.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Both have heard the exact same story. Their disagreement is about how to judge that story's credibility, not about the facts themselves.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Notice that Theseus and Hippolyta heard the same account. Their disagreement is not about what happened; it is about whether the story deserves belief.

questions.text:
Snug, playing the Lion, tells the audience before he even roars that he is really "Snug the joiner" and not a real lion. What storytelling mistake does this show?

Answers:

answers.text: He forgets his lines.
He removes the suspense by breaking the illusion before it can build.
He speaks in verse instead of prose.
He refuses to wear a costume.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. By announcing the lion is not real in advance, Snug takes away any suspense the moment might have had.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Think about what an audience needs in order to feel suspense, and what Snug does to that feeling before he has even acted.

questions.text:
The Prologue narrates the entire plot of Pyramus and Thisbe, including how it ends, while the actors silently act it out behind him. What does this show about strong storytelling?

Answers:

answers.text: Strong storytelling usually lets the audience notice things for themselves instead of explaining everything in advance.
Strong storytelling always uses a narrator to explain the plot.
Strong storytelling should never use stage directions.
Strong storytelling requires the ending to be a surprise for the actors.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The Prologue's mistake is explaining what the audience could discover on its own, including giving away the ending before it happens.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Think about what the Prologue takes away from the audience by telling them everything, including the ending, in advance.

questions.text:
Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

Answers:

answers.text: "The lion is not real" Snug said.
"The lion is not real," Snug said.
"The lion is not real", Snug said.
The lion is not real, Snug said.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. When a dialogue tag follows the spoken words, use a comma inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Review this week's dialogue punctuation patterns. The comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark, right after the last word of the spoken line.

questions.text:
A student wrote the following sentence. What is the error?

Theseus announced, "The play begins now".

Answers:

answers.text: There should be no comma after "announced."
The word "announced" should be capitalized.
The sentence does not need quotation marks.
The period belongs inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In American English, the period always goes inside the closing quotation mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Look carefully at where the period lands. It should sit inside the closing quotation mark, not after it.

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz: Commonly Confused Words and Proofreading and Editing (Week 6)

questions.text: "___ account of the night sounded believable to Hippolyta."

answers.text: There
They're
Their

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. This shows ownership (belonging to them), so it needs the possessive pronoun their.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask whether the sentence is showing ownership, naming a place, or shortening "they are." This one shows ownership.

questions.text: "I don't know if ___ true."

answers.text: it's
its
it

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Swap in "it is": "I don't know if it is true" still makes sense, so use the contraction it's.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Try swapping in "it is." If the sentence still makes sense, use the contraction it's.

questions.text: "This account is more convincing ___ that one."

answers.text: then
that's
than

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Two accounts are being compared, so this needs the comparing word than.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Then moves you forward in time. Than compares two things. This sentence is comparing.

questions.text: Which sentence uses your and you're correctly?

answers.text: Your the one who decides if you're outline is finished.
You're the one who decides if your outline is finished.
Your the one who decides if your outline is finished.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "You're" swaps in for "you are" (correct here), and "your" shows ownership of the outline.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Try swapping in "you are" wherever you see "you're." Your shows ownership.

questions.text: "puck speaks the final lines of the play." Which proofreading step catches the error in this sentence?

answers.text: Check confused words
Check capitals
Check end punctuation

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Puck is a proper name for a character, so it needs a capital letter.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look closely at the first word of the sentence. Is it capitalized correctly?

questions.text: "Theseus doubts the story, Hippolyta finds it convincing." Which proofreading step catches the error here?

answers.text: Check capitals
Check confused words
Check end punctuation

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two complete sentences are joined with only a comma. This needs a period, semicolon, or conjunction instead.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Count the complete sentences here. What is joining them, and is that enough?

questions.text: "The mechanicals performs their play for the whole court." Which proofreading step catches the error?

answers.text: Check end punctuation
Check subject and verb
Check capitals

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The subject "mechanicals" is plural, so the verb needs to match: "the mechanicals perform," not "performs."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the subject of the sentence. Is it one person or more than one? Does the verb match?

questions.text: Which sentence has no proofreading errors?

answers.text: Theseus does not believe the lovers' story at first.
theseus dont believe the lovers story at first.
Theseus don't believe the lover's story, at first he thinks its imagination.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. This sentence is capitalized correctly, uses the right confused word, and is properly punctuated.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check capitalization at the start of the sentence, subject-verb agreement, and whether "its" or "it's" is needed.

questions.text: In Act 1, what does Egeus accuse Lysander of doing?

answers.text: Stealing money from the family.
Bewitching Hermia and stealing her love away from Demetrius.
Refusing to speak to Hermia at all.
Breaking a promise to Theseus.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Egeus calls Lysander's courtship of Hermia bewitchment and theft, and asks Theseus to enforce the law against her.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Egeus's opening speech in Act 1, Scene 1. He describes Lysander's courtship in very unflattering terms.

questions.text: In Act 2, what does Titania claim has caused the strange, disordered seasons?

answers.text: A curse from a witch outside the fairy world.
Her quarrel with Oberon over the changeling boy.
The mortals traveling into the wood.
Puck's mischief with the love potion.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Titania states that the fairies' quarrel is the "parent" of the disordered seasons.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Titania's speech about the childing autumn and angry winter. She names the cause herself.

questions.text: In Act 3, what does Helena remind Hermia of, to try to save their friendship?

answers.text: A promise their parents made to each other.
Their shared childhood, growing up "like a double cherry."
A time Hermia saved her life.
A secret about Demetrius.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Helena describes their years of friendship, "two lovely berries moulded on one stem," as evidence Hermia should not betray now.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Helena's speech to Hermia in Act 3, Scene 2. She reaches for a shared memory.

questions.text: Why can Bottom not fully describe his night as a donkey loved by a fairy queen?

answers.text: He fell back asleep before he could think about it.
He insists no human sense or word could report what he saw.
He decides it was too embarrassing to tell anyone.
He forgets everything the instant he wakes up.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Bottom says the eye, ear, hand, and tongue of man are not able to report his dream, and then decides to have it made into a ballad anyway.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Bottom's speech right after he wakes in Act 4, Scene 1.

questions.text: In Act 5, why does Hippolyta think the lovers' account deserves some credit, even though Theseus doubts it?

answers.text: She was in the wood and saw it happen herself.
Four people telling the same strange, transformed story is itself a kind of evidence.
She does not actually believe it either.
Theseus asked her to agree with him.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Hippolyta argues that the story "grows to something of great constancy" because so many people tell it the same way.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Hippolyta's reply to Theseus at the start of Act 5, Scene 1.

questions.text: Why does the mechanicals' performance of Pyramus and Thisbe become funny instead of tragic?

answers.text: The actors refuse to perform at all.
Theseus stops the play before it finishes.
Clumsy verse, nervous actors, and odd staging choices undercut the story they meant to tell seriously.
The court falls asleep during the performance.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The mechanicals mean to move the court, but their awkward lines and staging turn the tragedy into comedy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the court's reactions during the performance. Are they moved, or amused?

questions.text: What is a frame, in the sense this module used the word?

answers.text: A picture hung on the wall of the stage set.
A story that closes by returning to the place, image, or words where it began.
Any story with more than one narrator.
A rule about how long a play must be.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A frame returns a story to its opening, marking exactly when it is over.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think back to Puck's epilogue and the poem "The Cremation of Sam McGee." What did both of them do at the end?

questions.text: What does Puck offer the audience at the end of his epilogue?

answers.text: A chance to ask the actors questions.
The choice to think of the whole play as a dream, if it offended them.
A promise that the mechanicals will perform again.
An apology from Oberon and Titania in person.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Puck tells the audience that if the play offended them, they may "think but this, and all is mended," that they only slumbered and dreamed it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opening lines of Puck's epilogue: "If we shadows have offended..."

questions.text: "___ going to perform the play again next week."

answers.text: Their
They're
There

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Swap in "they are": "they are going to perform the play again" makes sense, so use they're.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Try swapping in "they are." If it still makes sense, use they're.

questions.text: "The mechanicals performs their play for the whole court." Which proofreading step catches the error?

answers.text: Check capitals
Check end punctuation
Check subject and verb

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The subject "mechanicals" is plural, so the verb should be "perform," not "performs."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the subject. Is it one person or more than one? Does the verb agree with it?

quizzes.title: Module 4B Outro: A Midsummer Night's Dream
quizzes.description: This survey collects a refined answer to the module question, a confidence rating, and reflections on Module 4B. Honest answers show the teacher what landed and what to revisit.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your refined answer. Look back at how you answered this in the Module Intro: **Everyone in this play tells a story about what happened in the wood. Whose account can we trust, and how would we know?

Answer it again now, in three or four sentences, using something specific from the play (for example, Egeus's formal complaint, Titania's story about the changeling boy, Bottom's failed attempt to describe his vision, or Theseus and Hippolyta's disagreement about the lovers' account). How has your answer changed since the start?

(Survey, no scoring. Compare to the Q1 intro response to see growth.)
Confidence rating. How confident do you feel that you can explain whose account in A Midsummer Night's Dream deserves belief and back it up with evidence cited from the play?

answers.text: Very confident
Mostly confident
Somewhat confident
Not yet confident

questions.text:
What still feels unclear. Name one thing about the play, its characters, or the literary-analysis and citation skills in this module that still feels unclear or that you would like more practice with. If everything feels clear, say what you found hardest.

(Survey, free response. Teachers scan for common confusion points.)

Virtue reflection. Optima names seven virtues: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. This module is about the stories people tell, and about judging those stories fairly instead of automatically. Pick the ONE virtue the play most asked of its characters, and that this module asked of you:

answers.text: Honesty (telling a story that is true to what actually happened, even when a more flattering version is available)
Self-government (Hermia and Helena hold to their own judgment even under pressure from a father, a duke, or a friend)
Courtesy (Theseus chooses to receive even a badly told story with patience and generosity)
Another of the seven virtues

quizzes.title: Module 5 Intro: Short Story Unit
quizzes.description: Module 5 covers two suspense stories and a suspense story of the student's own. These questions give the teacher a starting point.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your first answer. Our question for this whole module is: **What makes a suspense story work: what we are told, or what we are not? How do writers use irony and the twist ending?

In two or three sentences, give a first answer, drawing on any suspense story, film, or game.

(Survey, no scoring. Used to compare against the Q1 response on the module outro.)

Module objectives: check each box to show you have read it. Module objectives:

- [ ] Read and follow the events of "The Most Dangerous Game" by Richard Connell. - [ ] Explain how situational and dramatic irony work, using examples from the story. - [ ] Identify the techniques a writer uses to build suspense: pacing, foreshadowing, and what is left unsaid. - [ ] Write a suspense short story with an ironic twist ending, plus a short author's note explaining your choices.

(Survey item. Acknowledgment, not a right answer; all boxes are correct to check.)
Group work opt-in. The final project can be done on your own or with one partner. Both paths get the same instructions and the same kind of feedback. Which do you want for this module?

answers.text: I will work on my own.
I would like to work with a partner (your teacher will help arrange this).
I am not sure yet; I will decide before the project opens.

questions.text:
A suspense story you already know. Name one suspense story, film, or book. In one or two sentences, describe the moment that felt most tense or surprising.

(Survey, no scoring. Light engagement signal that connects the module to the student's existing experience.)

(Multiple choice)

"He lived." is an example of what kind of sentence?

answers.text: A compound sentence
A fragment
A short, simple sentence used for dramatic effect
A run-on sentence

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It is a short, simple sentence. Its power comes from what comes before and after it in the story: the contrast is what makes it hit.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at how many words are in it and whether it has a subject and a verb. It is complete. Ask yourself what kind of sentence has exactly one subject and one verb with nothing extra.

questions.text:
(Multiple choice)

What is the subject noun in this sentence?

"Rainsford leaped up and grabbed a vine."

answers.text: leaped
vine
grabbed
Rainsford

questions.feedback_correct: Rainsford names the person the sentence is about, so it is the subject noun. Ask "Who or what leaped?" and the answer is Rainsford.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "Who or what leaped?" The answer to that question is the subject noun. It names the person performing the action.

questions.text:
(Multiple choice)

In that same sentence, what is the verb?

"Rainsford leaped up and grabbed a vine."

answers.text: leaped and grabbed
Rainsford
vine
up

questions.feedback_correct: Both action words tell what Rainsford did. When two verbs are joined by "and" and share the same subject, both count as the verb of the sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "What is being said about Rainsford?" Both action words answer that question. A sentence can have more than one verb when they are joined by a conjunction.

questions.text:
(Multiple choice)

A long sentence in a suspense story usually does which of the following?

answers.text: Confuses the reader and breaks concentration
Ends the scene quickly
Stretches a moment and layers detail, building tension
Removes all description from the scene

questions.feedback_correct: Long sentences slow the pace and add detail. In suspense writing, that layering can make dread build while the reader waits to find out what happens.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what happens when a writer adds more and more detail while you wait to find out what happens next. The delay itself is part of the effect.

questions.text:
(Multiple choice)

Which sentence best controls pacing at a scary moment?

answers.text: "He ran and he ran and he ran through the jungle until he was too tired to run anymore and then he stopped."
"He stopped."
"Running in the jungle at night is very dangerous."
"The jungle was dark and full of sounds."

questions.feedback_correct: The two-word sentence creates a jolt, like a jump cut in film. After a long chase, a short sentence carries the full weight of the moment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the shortest option and what effect the sudden stop would have on the reader. After tension, brevity hits harder.

questions.text:
(Multiple choice)

A comma placed in the middle of a suspense sentence can do which of the following?

answers.text: Always signals a list of three or more items
Signal a pause, slowing the reader down at a tense moment
End a sentence
Replace a period

questions.feedback_correct: Commas can force a micro-pause. Writers use that pause deliberately to build tension or to make the reader breathe carefully through a dangerous moment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what the reader must do physically when they hit a comma. It creates a brief stop. That stop is a tool the writer controls.

questions.text:
(Multiple choice)

In "He waited, listening, hardly breathing," what do the commas do?

answers.text: They list three things Rainsford owns.
They separate items in an unrelated list.
They slow the sentence into three separate beats, matching the stillness of waiting
They mark a direct quotation.

questions.feedback_correct: Each comma forces a pause. The sentence imitates the held breath of waiting: one beat, then another, then another. The punctuation and the meaning work together.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the sentence aloud and notice what your voice does at each comma. The pauses are not listing objects; they are mimicking the experience the character is having.

questions.text:
(Multiple choice)

An ellipsis (...) in dialogue or narration signals which of the following?

answers.text: A complete, finished thought
A trailing off, uncertainty, or a pause stretching into silence
The end of a chapter or section
A spelling error that needs correction

questions.feedback_correct: The ellipsis stretches a moment or shows a voice fading. In suspense writing, it is perfect for moments where the character (or the narrator) cannot quite complete the thought.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what happens when someone's voice trails off in the middle of a sentence. The ellipsis puts that experience on the page.

questions.text:
(Multiple choice)

Which sentence uses dashes to create a sharp interruption in a suspense moment?

answers.text: "The rain fell steadily."
"He heard something, a sound, from behind the tree."
"The branch snapped, and he fell."
"He turned the corner and stopped, his heart, his whole body, frozen."

questions.feedback_correct: The dashes interrupt the sentence, mimicking the sudden freeze of fear. The reader's eye stops at each dash the way a person stops when something frightens them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the sentence where something breaks the flow sharply, the way a sudden noise breaks silence. The correct answer uses pauses that feel like a physical jolt, not just a list or a conjunction.

questions.text:
(Multiple choice)

Which ending would best complete this sentence for maximum suspense?

"He reached for the door handle..."

answers.text: "and opened it easily."
"and found it locked."
"which was green."
"then went to bed."

questions.feedback_correct: The ellipsis sets up a pause and a sense of anticipation. The unexpected locked door pays it off with a surprise that raises the stakes. That combination of pause and reversal is a suspense technique.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about which ending creates the most surprise or dread after the ellipsis pause. The ellipsis promises something significant. Which ending delivers on that promise?

questions.text: What is the central situational irony of "The Most Dangerous Game"?

answers.text: Zaroff is friendly but secretly evil.
Rainsford, an expert hunter, becomes the hunted prey.
The island is more beautiful than expected.
Rainsford refuses to hunt.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The whole story turns on the irony of the hunter becoming the hunted.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Situational irony means the outcome is the opposite of what seemed right. Who is the hunter at the start of the story, and what happens to him?

questions.text: In "The Most Dangerous Game," what does General Zaroff hunt on his island?

answers.text: Big cats and bears.
Endangered birds.
Human beings.
Wild horses.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Zaroff is bored with animals and now hunts people, which he calls the "most dangerous game."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the dinner conversation between Rainsford and Zaroff.

questions.text: Dramatic irony means:

answers.text: The outcome is the opposite of what was expected.
Two characters disagree dramatically.
A character says one thing but means another.
The reader knows something a character does not.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Dramatic irony is the gap between what the reader knows and what the character understands.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the difference between what the reader suspects and what the character has admitted to themselves.

questions.text: "He lived." is an example of:

answers.text: A complex sentence with a dependent clause.
A comma splice.
A short, simple sentence used for dramatic impact.
A fragment missing a verb.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. It is a complete sentence with a subject and a verb. Its power comes from its brevity after so much tension.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Does the sentence have a subject and a verb? Is it complete? Then think about why Connell made it so short at that moment.

questions.text: In a suspense story, a long sentence is most useful for:

answers.text: Ending a scene quickly.
Replacing all short sentences.
Listing grammar rules.
Stretching a moment and layering detail to build tension.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A long sentence slows the reader and adds detail, which can stretch the moment of suspense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what a reader must do to get through a long sentence, and how that slowing of pace can build dread.

questions.text: In "He waited, listening, hardly breathing," what do the commas do?

answers.text: They mark the end of a sentence.
They separate items in an unrelated grocery list.
They slow the sentence into three separate beats, matching the stillness of waiting.
They introduce a quotation.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Each comma forces a pause. The sentence imitates a held breath.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the sentence aloud. What do the commas make your voice do?

questions.text: An ellipsis (...) in suspense writing usually signals:

answers.text: A complete, finished thought.
A spelling mistake.
A loud, sudden noise.
A trailing off, a pause, or something left unsaid.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The ellipsis stretches a moment or lets a voice fade, leaving the reader in silence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what happens when someone's voice trails off before finishing a sentence.

questions.text: In "The Landlady," what clues suggest that something is very wrong, even though the landlady seems kind?

answers.text: She charges too much for the room.
The pets are taxidermied, the register holds only two names Billy half-recognizes, and the tea tastes odd.
The house is filthy and cold.
Billy is rude to her.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. These details are Dahl's foreshadowing: clues that something terrible is happening under the surface.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the small, specific details Dahl includes about the room, the animals, and the other guests.

questions.text: Foreshadowing means:

answers.text: A character makes a prediction about the weather.
Clues or hints early in a story that point toward what will happen later.
A summary of events at the end of a chapter.
A moment when a character lies.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Foreshadowing plants early clues that pay off later, often making the reader feel dread before they can explain why.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what a "shadow" cast before an event would mean: something that hints at what is coming.

questions.text: Both "The Most Dangerous Game" and "The Landlady" end with something the writer does NOT say directly. What technique does this use?

answers.text: Flashback.
Simile.
Letting the reader infer the conclusion from what came before.
Direct address.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both stories withhold the final reveal and trust the reader to infer it from the clues already planted.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what both stories leave out at the very end, and how you knew what happened even though it was not stated.

quizzes.title: Module 5 Outro: Short Story Unit
quizzes.description: The reading and project work for Module 5 is complete. These questions look back at what was read, noticed, and written. Honest answers show the teacher what landed and what to revisit.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your refined answer. The Module Intro asked: **What makes a suspense story work: what we are told, or what we are not? How do writers use irony and the twist ending?

Answer it again, in three or four sentences, using something specific from "The Most Dangerous Game." Explain how the answer has changed since the start of the module.

(Survey, no scoring. Compare to the Q1 intro response to see growth.)
Confidence rating. How confident are you in explaining how irony and suspense work in a short story and using those techniques in your own writing?

answers.text: Very confident
Mostly confident
Somewhat confident
Not yet confident

questions.text:
What still feels unclear. Name one thing about irony, suspense, the twist ending, or the writing skills in this module that still feels unclear or that you would like more practice with. If everything feels clear, say what you found hardest.

(Survey, free response. Teachers scan for common confusion points.)

Virtue reflection. Optima names seven virtues: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. Writing a suspense story asks something of the writer. Pick the ONE virtue this module asked for most:

answers.text: Perseverance (staying with a hard draft until the story works)
Self-government (planning your plot and pacing rather than rushing to the ending)
Honesty (writing a twist that is fair to the reader, not a cheat)
Another of the seven virtues

quizzes.title: Module 6 Intro: The Scarlet Pimpernel
quizzes.description: Module 6 covers The Scarlet Pimpernel by Baroness Orczy, a novel set during the French Revolution. A mysterious English hero, known only as the Scarlet Pimpernel, risks his life again and again to rescue French aristocrats from the guillotine. No one knows who he is. A few quick questions come first. First responses give the teacher a starting point.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your first answer. Our question for this whole module is: **Heroism in disguise: what kind of courage does the novel celebrate, and when is it right to risk everything for strangers?

In two or three sentences, give your first answer. You have not read the book yet, so say what you think: when do you believe it is right to put yourself at risk for people you do not know, and is that courage, foolishness, or something else?

(Survey, no scoring. Used to compare against the Q1 response on the module outro.)

Module objectives: check each box to show you have read it. By the end of this module you will be able to:

- [ ] Read all thirty-one chapters of The Scarlet Pimpernel and trace the plot from the Paris barricades to the final escape. - [ ] Explain how Orczy uses disguise and identity to build both suspense and theme. - [ ] Notice and name craft moves such as irony, foreshadowing, and point of view, and connect them to meaning. - [ ] Build one argumentative essay step by step: a thesis, evidence with explanation, a counterargument, and a conclusion. - [ ] Write an argumentative essay and create a creative component about heroism and disguise.

(Survey item. Acknowledgment, not a right answer; all boxes are correct to check.)
Group work opt-in. The final project can be done on your own or with one partner. Both paths get the same instructions and the same kind of feedback. Which do you want for this module?

answers.text: I will work on my own.
I would like to work with a partner (your teacher will help arrange this).
I am not sure yet; I will decide before the project opens.

questions.text:
One thing you are curious about. Name one thing about the French Revolution, about heroes who hide their identity, or about this novel that you are curious to find out. One sentence is fine.

(Survey, no scoring. Light engagement signal.)

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 1: Passive Voice and Sentence Variety)

questions.text: In which sentence is the verb in passive voice?

answers.text: Bibot laughed until his sides ached.
The crowd rushed toward the barricade.
The sergeants had been threatened with death.
Sally carried the tankards to the tables.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The subject (the sergeants) receives the action. "Had been threatened" is the signal: a helping verb plus a past participle, with the doer not named.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In a passive sentence, the subject receives the action rather than doing it. Look for a helping verb like was, were, or had been paired with a past participle.

questions.text: Which word in this sentence is the subject noun? "The crowd rushed away from the barricade."

answers.text: rushed
away
barricade
crowd

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Crowd names the group that does the action. Ask "who or what rushed?" and the answer is the subject noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "who or what rushed?" The answer to that question is the subject noun.

questions.text: A passive sentence almost always contains:

answers.text: two independent clauses joined by a conjunction.
a dependent clause beginning with because or although.
a form of "to be" (was, were, had been) plus a past participle.
a subject pronoun followed by an action verb.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Was doubled," "had been threatened," "were sent": the helping verb + past participle pattern signals passive voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about what the verb phrase looks like in a passive sentence. It has two parts: a form of "to be" and a past participle.

questions.text: Which sentence is a SIMPLE sentence?

answers.text: Bibot laughed so much, and the tears streamed down his cheeks.
Sally looked cross for a moment.
The crowd rushed away because the captain had shouted.
The guards doubled their watch, but the cart had already left.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. One subject noun (Sally), one verb (looked), one complete thought. A simple sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A simple sentence has one independent clause: one subject and one predicate. Which option has only that?

questions.text: "Bibot laughed until his sides ached, and the tears streamed down his cheeks." What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Complex
Compound
Neither

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two independent clauses are joined by the conjunction "and." Each part could stand alone as a complete sentence. That is a compound sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the conjunction joining two complete clauses. Can you split the sentence at that conjunction and get two sentences that each stand alone?

questions.text: Which word in a compound sentence joins the two independent clauses?

answers.text: subject noun
conjunction
object of the preposition
article adjective

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A conjunction (and, but, or, so, yet) joins the two independent clauses in a compound sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the connecting word that glues two complete thoughts together in a compound sentence.

questions.text: "The women spent their day on the square, whilst they watched the tumbrils arrive." What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Compound
Neither
Complex

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Whilst they watched" is a dependent clause: it has a subject (they) and a verb (watched), but it cannot stand alone. A dependent clause attached to a main independent clause makes a complex sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the word "whilst." It signals a dependent clause, one that cannot stand alone. When a dependent clause is attached to an independent clause, the result is a complex sentence.

questions.text: In a passive sentence, the subject noun or subject pronoun:

answers.text: does the action.
receives the action.
is always unnamed.
always comes after the verb.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In passive voice, the subject receives the action rather than performing it. The doer is often unnamed or appears after "by."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Active voice: the subject does the action. Passive voice: the subject receives it. Which one fits the description of passive?

questions.text: Who is the author of The Scarlet Pimpernel, and when was it published?

answers.text: Charles Dickens, 1843
Emma Orczy, 1905
Jack London, 1903
Richard Connell, 1924

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Baroness Emma Orczy published it in 1905, set over a century before in 1792.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Those are authors from other modules. The author of The Scarlet Pimpernel is Baroness Orczy.

questions.text: In Chapter 1, where does the story open?

answers.text: A warm English inn in Dover.
A farmhouse outside London.
The West Barricade in Paris.
The home of the Comtesse de Tourney.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Chapter 1 opens at the West Barricade of Paris in September 1792, where Sergeant Bibot is on guard.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look back at the first paragraph of Chapter 1. What location and time of day does Orczy describe?

questions.text: How does the Scarlet Pimpernel outwit Sergeant Bibot in the story Bibot tells at the barricade?

answers.text: He swims across the river.
He disguises himself as Bibot's commanding officer and leads the aristos away.
He bribes the guards with gold.
He hides inside a barrel.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. In Bibot's tale, the Pimpernel posed as the captain of the guard, and his "soldiers" were actually the aristos he was rescuing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the story Bibot tells about what happened at the North Gate. The real twist comes at the end of the story.

questions.text: How did the Comtesse de Tourney and her children escape at the end of Chapter 1?

answers.text: In a cart driven by an old woman who claimed her grandson had the plague.
Hidden inside barrels of wine.
Disguised as soldiers.
In a carriage belonging to Lord Tony.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The Pimpernel used the threat of smallpox and plague to scatter the crowd and get the cart through the gate.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the end of Chapter 1. What made the crowd step back and let the cart pass?

questions.text: In Chapter 2, the Fisherman's Rest is located in:

answers.text: Paris, France.
Dover, England.
London, England.
Calais, France.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Fisherman's Rest is an inn in Dover, England, on the English side of the Channel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Chapter 2's title is "Dover: The Fisherman's Rest." Which country is Dover in?

questions.text: Which sentence is in PASSIVE voice?

answers.text: Bibot laughed at his own story.
The crowd rushed toward the barricades.
The guards at the gates had been doubled.
Sally carried the tankards to the tables.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The guards receive the action: "had been doubled." The doer is not named. That is the signal for passive voice.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In a passive sentence, the subject receives the action. Look for a helping verb like "had been" plus a past participle.

questions.text: "Bibot laughed until his sides ached, and the tears streamed down his cheeks." What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple
Complex
Compound
Neither

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two independent clauses joined by the conjunction "and." Each part could stand on its own. That is a compound sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the conjunction joining the two clauses. Can you split the sentence at that word and get two complete sentences? If so, it is compound.

questions.text: In a compound sentence, the two independent clauses are joined by a:

answers.text: subject noun
object of the preposition
article adjective
conjunction

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A conjunction (and, but, or, so, yet) joins the two independent clauses in a compound sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the connecting word between the two complete thoughts in a compound sentence. What part of speech does that joining word belong to?

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz: Types of Sentences + Compound and Complex Sentences (Week 2)

questions.text: A sentence that states a fact or idea and ends with a period is called:

answers.text: An imperative sentence
An exclamatory sentence
A declarative sentence
An interrogative sentence

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. A declarative sentence states a fact or idea and ends with a period.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the four types and what each one does. A statement of fact ends with a period and is a declarative sentence.

questions.text: Which sentence from the novel is an INTERROGATIVE sentence?

answers.text: "Welcome! Welcome to old England!" (Ch. 3)
"What is the Scarlet Pimpernel, Monsieur?" (Ch. 4)
"Hush!" (Ch. 3)
"The Scarlet Pimpernel works in the dark." (Ch. 4)

questions.feedback_correct: Right. An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the sentence that asks something. An interrogative sentence ends with a question mark.

questions.text: In an IMPERATIVE sentence, the subject is usually:

answers.text: The narrator
A named character
Understood to be "you" and not stated
Always stated twice

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. In an imperative sentence, the subject you is understood but not written out. The sentence gives a command or request.
questions.feedback_incorrect: An imperative sentence gives a command. The person being commanded is you, even when that word does not appear.

questions.text: "Off with you, my pretty Sally, and see how quick you can dish up the soup." (Ch. 3) What type of sentence is this?

answers.text: Declarative
Interrogative
Exclamatory
Imperative

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Lord Antony is giving a command. The subject you is understood. That is an imperative sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Is someone being told to do something? A command with an understood subject you is an imperative sentence.

questions.text: A COMPOUND sentence joins two independent clauses with:

answers.text: A subordinating conjunction such as "because" or "although"
A coordinating conjunction such as "and," "but," or "so"
A period followed by a new sentence
A dependent clause that cannot stand alone

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so, for, yet, nor) or a semicolon.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Remember: compound uses coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, so). Complex uses subordinating conjunctions (because, although, when, if).

questions.text: Which sentence from the novel is a COMPOUND sentence?

answers.text: "Although she was insulted, Marguerite kept her composure."
"Because he was wealthy, society accepted him."
"Everyone heard it and paused instinctively." (Ch. 5)
"While Suzanne watched, the Comtesse turned away."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Everyone heard it" and "everyone paused" are two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction "and." That is a compound sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction like "and." Both halves should be able to stand alone.

questions.text: "She was crying gently to herself, whilst Suzanne ran up to her." (Ch. 4) This sentence is complex because:

answers.text: It has two subjects
"Whilst" is a subordinating conjunction that introduces a dependent clause
It is very long
It uses a semicolon

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Whilst" is a subordinating conjunction. The clause it introduces depends on the main clause and cannot stand alone. That makes the sentence complex.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask: can "whilst Suzanne ran up to her" stand alone as a complete sentence? No. A clause that cannot stand alone is a dependent clause, and that makes the whole sentence complex.

questions.text: "Sir Percy seemed very proud of his clever wife, and society could never do more than guess at it." What is the structure of this sentence?

answers.text: Simple sentence
Complex sentence
Compound sentence
Declarative only

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Both halves are independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction "and." That is a compound sentence. It is also declarative in type, but its structure is compound.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the conjunction and check whether both sides can stand alone. Two independent clauses plus a coordinating conjunction equals a compound sentence.

questions.text: In Chapter 3, who are the people arriving at the Fisherman's Rest, and why are they there?

answers.text: British spies coming to arrest Lord Antony.
French aristocrats escaping the Revolution.
Members of the Scarlet Pimpernel's League on a mission.
A traveling theater company performing for the landlord.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The refugees fleeing France are French aristocrats who have escaped the guillotine and need safe passage in England.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opening of Chapter 3. The strangers arriving at the inn are trying to escape France.

questions.text: In Chapter 4, the Comtesse de Tournay refuses to greet Lady Blakeney. What does this moment tell us about Marguerite?

answers.text: Marguerite is not actually English.
Marguerite is disliked by English society.
Marguerite once gave information that harmed a French family.
Marguerite is the leader of the League.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The Comtesse snubs Marguerite because Marguerite once denounced the St. Cyr family. That is the past action hanging over her.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Comtesse would not snub the most celebrated woman in England without a specific reason. What did we learn about Marguerite and the St. Cyr family in Chapter 4?

questions.text: In Chapter 6, how does society describe Sir Percy Blakeney?

answers.text: As a man of hidden talent and fierce loyalty.
As the most dangerous enemy of the French Republic.
As a coward who lets other men take risks for him.
As an extremely wealthy man considered hopelessly stupid.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Chapter 6 tells us society considers Percy wealthy, fashionable, and "hopelessly stupid." That is the mask he wears.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opening of Chapter 6, where the narrator describes how London society sees Percy.

questions.text: Characterization is the way a writer builds a character. Which of the following is an example of INDIRECT characterization?

answers.text: The narrator says that Percy is one of the wealthiest men in England.
Sir Andrew notices Percy's expression shift to show "intense longing, deep and hopeless passion."
The narrator names Percy as the Scarlet Pimpernel.
The novel states that Percy married Marguerite two years before the story begins.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Indirect characterization shows us something about a character through actions or reactions, without the narrator stating it outright. Sir Andrew observing Percy's look is the reader seeing something the rest of society misses.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Direct characterization is when the narrator tells you something about a character directly. Indirect characterization shows you something through actions, reactions, or small observed details rather than a plain statement.

questions.text: A sentence that gives a command or makes a request is called:

answers.text: A declarative sentence.
An interrogative sentence.
A compound sentence.
An imperative sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. An imperative sentence gives a command or request. The subject you is usually understood rather than stated.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the four sentence types. Which one gives a command?

questions.text: "She was crying gently to herself, whilst Suzanne ran up to her." (Ch. 4) What kind of sentence is this?

answers.text: Simple sentence.
Compound sentence.
Complex sentence.
Exclamatory sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Whilst" is a subordinating conjunction. The clause "whilst Suzanne ran up to her" cannot stand alone, making this a complex sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the conjunction. Does it join two independent clauses (compound), or does it introduce a dependent clause that cannot stand alone (complex)?

questions.text: Which sentence from this week is a COMPOUND sentence?

answers.text: "May God protect you all, Messieurs." (Ch. 4)
"Everyone heard it and paused instinctively." (Ch. 5)
"Although she was insulted, Marguerite kept her composure."
"Blakeney was the prince of good fellows."

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Everyone heard it" and "everyone paused" are two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction "and." That is a compound sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction like "and," "but," or "so." Which sentence has two parts that could each stand alone?

questions.text: In Chapters 3 through 6, Baroness Orczy gives readers two different pictures of Percy Blakeney. What is the effect of that contrast?

answers.text: It shows that Percy is lying to his wife.
It creates a mystery that makes readers want to find out what Percy is hiding.
It suggests Percy is not an important character.
It proves society's opinion is correct.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The gap between what society sees (a foolish dandy) and what Sir Andrew briefly glimpses (intensity, passion) is exactly the kind of dramatic contrast that keeps a reader asking questions. That is how Orczy builds suspense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Why would a novelist go to the trouble of building two portraits of the same character? Think about what it does to the reader.

quizzes.title: Grammar POP Quiz: Commonly Confused Words I & II

questions.text:
Select the sentence that uses the underlined word correctly.

Which sentence correctly uses their?

answers.text: The two young men sat in their usual corner of the coffee-room.
Their is a masked figure moving along the floor.
They forgot their from the novel's opening scene.
Percy said he would meet them their by the fire.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Their" is a possessive pronoun showing the corner belonged to the two men.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Their" is a possessive pronoun. Look for the sentence where the word shows ownership.

questions.text:
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.

"Marguerite looked out at the sea; she knew that _____ was little she could do to help Armand now."

answers.text: there
their
they're
thier

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "There" introduces a statement about existence. "There was little she could do."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each option. "Their" shows ownership. "They're" means "they are." "Thier" is a spelling error. Which one introduces a statement about a situation?

questions.text: Select the sentence that uses the underlined word correctly.

answers.text: Chauvelin smiled, knowing they're letters would betray Armand.
The League members did not know they're being followed.
Lord Tony and Sir Andrew are loyal; they're willing to risk everything.
The papers were taken from they're hiding place.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "They're" means "they are," and it works here: "they are willing to risk everything."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Try replacing "they're" with "they are" in each sentence. The sentence that still makes sense is the correct one.

questions.text:
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.

"Marguerite, is that _____ final word on the matter?" Chauvelin asked quietly.

answers.text: you're
your
yore
you are

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Your" is a possessive pronoun. The word belongs to Marguerite.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Your" shows possession. "You're" means "you are." Try reading the sentence with "you are" in place of the blank. Does it sound right?

questions.text: Select the sentence that uses the underlined word correctly.

answers.text: "You're courage is remarkable," Percy told Marguerite.
"You're going to help me tonight," Chauvelin said.
Marguerite knew you're brother had been arrested.
The note with you're red flower was in Chauvelin's hand.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "You're" means "you are." The sentence reads: "You are going to help me tonight."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Replace "you're" with "you are" in each sentence. Which one still makes sense?

questions.text:
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.

"The figure paused, then continued _____ way across the dark floor of the inn."

answers.text: it's
its
its'
its's

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Its" is a possessive pronoun. The way belongs to the figure.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Its" shows possession. "It's" always means "it is." Try reading the sentence with "it is" in place of the blank. Does it sound right?

questions.text: Select the sentence that uses the underlined word correctly.

answers.text: Armand knew it's dangerous to carry letters into France.
The Daydream made it's way out of the harbor at dawn.
The novel's tension comes from its impossible choices.
The League has it's headquarters somewhere in England.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Its" is a possessive pronoun. The tension belongs to the novel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Replace "it's" with "it is" wherever you see it. If the sentence stops making sense, "its" (no apostrophe) is the right choice.

questions.text:
Choose the word or words that correctly complete the sentence.

"Marguerite had _____ choices, and both were _____ terrible _____ name."

answers.text: two / too / to
to / two / too
too / to / two
two / to / too

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Two" counts a number; "too" means "also" or "to an excessive degree"; "to" is a preposition.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each blank. The first blank counts how many choices. The second blank means "excessively" before an adjective. The third blank introduces the infinitive form of a verb.

questions.text: What does Marguerite tell Armand about the arrest of the Marquis de St. Cyr's family?

answers.text: She denies any involvement in the arrest.
She says Percy ordered the arrest to protect the League.
She reveals that she gave Chauvelin information that led to the family's arrest, believing the St. Cyrs had betrayed Armand.
She tells Armand the arrest was a rumor and no one was harmed.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Marguerite explains that she gave Chauvelin a piece of information about the St. Cyrs, not fully understanding what it would cost them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread Chapter 7. Marguerite is honest with Armand about her role in the St. Cyr arrest.

questions.text: Where does Chauvelin approach Marguerite to make his first request in Chapter 8?

answers.text: In the Blakeney drawing room in London
Outside the Fisherman's Rest inn at Dover
At the Covent Garden opera house
On the dock as the Daydream sets sail

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Chauvelin finds Marguerite outside the Fisherman's Rest and introduces himself as France's accredited agent.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Chapter 8 takes place at Dover, near the inn where the story opened.

questions.text: What does Marguerite say when Chauvelin first asks her to identify the Scarlet Pimpernel?

answers.text: She says she does not know who the Pimpernel is.
She refuses, calling him brave and noble and saying she would never help with such villainy.
She agrees to help and asks Chauvelin for more time.
She tells Chauvelin to ask Percy instead.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Marguerite's exact refusal includes calling whoever the Pimpernel is "brave and noble."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Go back to Chapter 8. Marguerite is not passive at this first meeting.

questions.text: What does Chauvelin discover when he seizes the papers from Lord Tony and Sir Andrew in Chapter 9?

answers.text: A map showing the Scarlet Pimpernel's escape route through France
A letter signed by Percy Blakeney, confirming he is the Pimpernel
A letter from Armand St. Just proving he is working with the Scarlet Pimpernel
A list of all the League members' real names

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The seized letter is from Armand, and it gives Chauvelin the leverage he needs over Marguerite.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Chapter 9 focuses on what Chauvelin finds in the papers he takes from the two young League members.

questions.text: In Chapter 10, what ultimatum does Chauvelin give Marguerite at the opera?

answers.text: Spy for him at Grenville's ball tonight, or Armand will be arrested and sent to the guillotine.
Reveal Percy's secrets, or she will be arrested at the opera house.
Travel to France with him immediately, or Armand will be executed at dawn.
Sign a letter condemning the Scarlet Pimpernel, or Armand's letter will be sent to the Committee.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Chauvelin shows Marguerite the note with the red flower device, tells her the Pimpernel will attend Grenville's ball, and demands she spy for him that night.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the opera-box scene in Chapter 10. Chauvelin has a specific location and a specific night in mind.

questions.text: Choose the sentence that uses "there," "their," and "they're" correctly.

answers.text: Their going to meet the Pimpernel over their, in the shadows.
There is no doubt that they're prepared to risk their lives.
They're going to wait they're for they're contact.
Chauvelin watched there movements; their was something suspicious about them.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "There" introduces a fact; "they're" means "they are"; "their" shows possession.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Test each word by substituting its full meaning: "there" = that place or "there is/are"; "they're" = "they are"; "their" = belonging to them.

questions.text: Choose the sentence that uses "its" and "it's" correctly.

answers.text: The novel makes it's argument through Marguerite's impossible choice; its a story about loyalty under pressure.
The story has it's climax in the opera box; it's clear Marguerite has no good options.
The novel's climax is in the opera box; its clear that its impossible choice drives the plot.
The opera scene makes its argument through an impossible choice; it's the moment Marguerite's loyalty is truly tested.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Its" (no apostrophe) shows the argument belongs to the opera scene; "it's" = "it is."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Replace every "it's" with "it is." If the sentence still makes sense, "it's" is correct. "Its" (no apostrophe) always shows possession.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses "to," "too," and "two"?

answers.text: Marguerite had to choose between two loyalties; the cost was too high either way.
Marguerite had too choose between to loyalties; the cost was two high either way.
Marguerite had two choose between to loyalties; the cost was too high either way.
Marguerite had to choose between too loyalties; the cost was two high either way.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "To" before a verb; "two" counts a number; "too" means "excessively."
questions.feedback_incorrect: "To" goes before a verb. "Two" counts a number (like "twin" has a "w"). "Too" means "also" or "excessively" (it has an extra "o" because it means extra).

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 4: Commonly Confused Words III and Subject-Verb Agreement)

questions.text: Which sentence uses affect correctly?

answers.text: The cold weather had no affect on his plans.
Her courage will affect the outcome.
The affect of the storm was damage.
He walked than sat down.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Affect is a verb here, meaning to influence. You could replace it with "influence" and the sentence still works.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Affect is almost always a verb. If you can replace the word with "influence," you want affect.

questions.text: Which sentence uses effect correctly?

answers.text: The medicine will effect her quickly.
She could effect the crowd with her voice.
The effect of the news was stunned silence.
He is smarter then anyone else.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Effect is a noun here, naming the result. You could replace it with "result" and the sentence still works.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Effect is almost always a noun naming a result. Try the swap: if "result" fits, use effect.

questions.text: Which word correctly completes this sentence? "Sir Percy was wealthier ___ anyone else in the room."

answers.text: then
effect
affect
than

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Than signals a comparison between two things: Sir Percy compared to everyone else.
questions.feedback_incorrect: This sentence compares two things. When you compare, use than.

questions.text: Which word correctly completes this sentence? "Marguerite read the note, ___ she slipped it behind her."

answers.text: affect
then
than
effect

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Then signals sequence: one action followed another.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The sentence moves through steps in time, not a comparison. Use then for time order.

questions.text: Which sentence has NO error with affect, effect, than, or then?

answers.text: The long drive had a strange affect on her.
She arrived later then expected.
He was calmer then she was.
Chauvelin waited, then smiled slowly.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Then is used correctly for time sequence. No errors.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each sentence: affect/effect swap test, than/then comparison vs. sequence.

questions.text: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?

answers.text: The members of the League is daring men.
Each of the men carry a secret.
The crowd of guests fills the ballroom.
Sir Percy and Chauvelin watches each other.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The subject noun is crowd (singular), so the verb fills is singular too.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the subject noun: not a word in a prepositional phrase. Then check whether the verb matches it.

questions.text: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?

answers.text: Chauvelin and Marguerite is at the ball.
The notes in the scrap of paper was burned.
The Scarlet Pimpernel and his league rescue French aristocrats.
Everyone in the grand rooms admire him.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Two subject nouns joined by and take a plural verb: "rescue" agrees with "the Scarlet Pimpernel and his league."
questions.feedback_incorrect: When two subjects are joined by and, use a plural verb.

questions.text: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?

answers.text: Each of the guests were watching the door.
The guests in the ballroom were watching the door.
The music, along with the laughter, drown out his words.
Neither Percy nor Marguerite speak during the drive.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The subject noun guests is plural, so the verb were is plural.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the true subject noun. Phrases like "along with" or "of the guests" are not the subject.

questions.text: What is the subject noun in this sentence? "The pages of the letter tell Chauvelin everything."

answers.text: letter
Chauvelin
pages
everything

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Ask "Who or what tell?" The answer is pages, not letter. Letter is the object of the preposition of.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Nouns inside a prepositional phrase are objects of the preposition, not the subject. Ask "Who or what [verb]?"

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a singular verb with an indefinite subject?

answers.text: Everyone at the ball know the doggerel verse.
Nobody in the rooms notice Chauvelin's plan.
Someone in the shadows watches every move.
Each of the spies were ready.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Indefinite pronouns like someone, everyone, nobody, and each take a singular verb.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Words like someone, everyone, nobody, and each are singular. They take a singular verb even when followed by a prepositional phrase with a plural noun.

questions.text: At the ball in Chapter 11, what does Sir Percy Blakeney do that entertains everyone?

answers.text: He challenges Chauvelin to a duel.
He recites a doggerel verse mocking the French search for the Pimpernel.
He reveals the Pimpernel's identity to the Prince of Wales.
He slips a secret note to Sir Andrew Ffoulkes.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Percy delivers the famous quatrain about seeking the Pimpernel "everywhere" to general amusement.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look back at Ch 11 and the reaction of the crowd to Sir Percy's performance at the ball.

questions.text: What two pieces of information does Marguerite read on Sir Andrew's scrap of paper before it is burned?

answers.text: The Pimpernel's real name and the location of his ship.
A list of French aristocrats the Pimpernel plans to rescue.
"Start myself tomorrow" and a plan to meet in the supper-room at one o'clock.
The address of a safe house in Calais and a date for a crossing.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. She reads these two fragments before Sir Andrew destroys the note.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the boudoir scene in Ch 12. What two lines does Marguerite manage to make out?

questions.text: At the end of Chapter 14, who is in the supper-room when Chauvelin's trap springs at one o'clock?

answers.text: The Scarlet Pimpernel and two of his agents.
Sir Andrew Ffoulkes, who has been warned.
Only Chauvelin and the sleeping Sir Percy Blakeney.
No one -- the room is completely empty.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Chauvelin finds only himself and Sir Percy Blakeney, apparently fast asleep, in the corner.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the end of Ch 14. Who does Chauvelin find when he settles in to wait?

questions.text: Dramatic irony occurs when:

answers.text: Two characters argue about the same event.
A character finds out a secret and tells everyone.
The ending of the story is a complete surprise to the reader.
The reader knows something that a character in the story does not.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Dramatic irony is the gap between what the reader knows and what the characters understand.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reread the lesson on dramatic irony. What word describes the gap between the reader's knowledge and the characters' knowledge?

questions.text: Which sentence uses "affect" and "than" correctly?

answers.text: The cold night air had a strange effect than she expected.
She felt worst then she had before, do to the affect of the news.
The affected tone of the speech was worse then anything she had heard.
The decision affected her more than she wanted to admit.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Affected" is the verb (to influence), and "than" signals the comparison.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each word: affect/effect swap test, than/then comparison vs. sequence.

questions.text: In Chapter 16, what does Sir Percy do after Marguerite goes inside the house at Richmond?

answers.text: He kneels and kisses the steps where she had walked.
He rides off immediately to begin the rescue of Armand.
He writes a letter to Chauvelin threatening him.
He calls her back and asks for forgiveness.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. In the last paragraphs of Ch 16, Percy kneels on the terrace steps and kisses the places where Marguerite's feet had rested.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Read the final paragraphs of Ch 16 carefully. What does Percy do the moment Marguerite is out of sight?

questions.text: What is the subject noun in this sentence? "The leader of the agents speaks for the whole group."

answers.text: agents
group
whole
leader

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Ask "Who or what speaks?" The answer is "leader" (singular). "Agents" is the object of the preposition "of."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Nouns inside a prepositional phrase are objects of the preposition, not the subject. Ask "Who or what performs the verb?"

questions.text: Which sentence has correct subject-verb agreement?

answers.text: Sir Percy and Marguerite talks on the terrace.
The members of the League is very loyal.
Neither the trap nor Chauvelin's plans succeed that night.
Everyone in the room know the secret verse.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the noun closest to it. "Plans" is the closer noun (plural), so "succeed" is plural.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the subject of each sentence carefully. Remember: words inside prepositional phrases are not the subject, and compound subjects joined by "and" take a plural verb.

questions.text:
Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement

Question: In the sentence "Percy kissed her hand and rode away," what is the antecedent of her?

- A. Percy - B. hand - C. Marguerite (implied from context) - D. rode

Correct answer: C

Per-answer feedback: - A: Incorrect. Percy is the subject performing the action, not the antecedent of her. - B: Incorrect. Hand is a noun in the sentence, but it is not the person the pronoun refers to. - C: Correct. Her refers to Marguerite; it is singular feminine, matching its antecedent. - D: Incorrect. Rode is a verb, not a noun antecedent.

Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement

Question: Which sentence has pronoun-antecedent agreement?

- A. The groom took his horse and left. - B. The groom took their horse and left. - C. The grooms took his horse and left. - D. The groom took its horse and left.

Correct answer: A

Per-answer feedback: - A: Correct. His is singular masculine, matching groom, which is singular masculine. Good agreement. - B: Incorrect. Their is plural; groom is singular. That is a mismatch. - C: Incorrect. His is singular; grooms is plural. Mismatch. - D: Incorrect. Its refers to a thing or animal, not a person.

Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement

Question: "Marguerite looked at Suzanne and smiled at __." Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence?

- A. them - B. her - C. him - D. it

Correct answer: B

Per-answer feedback: - A: Incorrect. Them is plural; Suzanne is one person. - B: Correct. Her is singular feminine, matching the antecedent Suzanne. - C: Incorrect. Him is masculine; Suzanne is female. - D: Incorrect. It refers to things, not people.

Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement

Question: Which pronoun error, if any, appears in this sentence? "Neither Percy nor Marguerite could hide their fear."

- A. No error: their is acceptable here because two people are mentioned. - B. Their should be his. - C. Their should be its. - D. Their should be them.

Correct answer: A

Per-answer feedback: - A: Correct. When two people are joined by neither/nor, the pronoun typically agrees with the nearer noun (Marguerite, singular); however, their is widely accepted in this construction and creates no practical confusion. No revision is required. - B: Incorrect. His would refer only to Percy; the sentence covers both characters. - C: Incorrect. Its refers to things, not people. - D: Incorrect. Them is an object pronoun, not a possessive pronoun.

Consistent Verb Tense

Question: Which sentence has consistent verb tense?

- A. Marguerite opened the door and sees the horses. - B. Marguerite opens the door and sees the horses. - C. Marguerite opened the door and see the horses. - D. Marguerite opens the door and saw the horses.

Correct answer: B

Per-answer feedback: - A: Incorrect. Opened is past tense; sees is present tense. Tense shift. - B: Correct. Both verbs are present tense: consistent. - C: Incorrect. Opened is past tense; see is present tense. Tense shift. - D: Incorrect. Opens is present tense; saw is past tense. Tense shift.

Consistent Verb Tense

Question: Identify the tense shift: "Sir Andrew rides to Dover and reached the inn by midnight."

- A. Rides (present) shifts to reached (past). - B. Dover is spelled incorrectly. - C. By midnight is an error. - D. There is no error.

Correct answer: A

Per-answer feedback: - A: Correct. Rides is present tense; reached is past tense. Pick one tense: either rides/reaches or rode/reached. - B: Incorrect. The spelling of Dover is not the issue here. - C: Incorrect. The phrase by midnight is fine; the tense mismatch is the problem. - D: Incorrect. Rides is present tense; reached is past tense. That is an inconsistency.

Consistent Verb Tense

Question: When writing a paragraph about what happens in Chapter 22, which tense should you use throughout?
