- A. Future tense - B. Present tense - C. Past tense - D. It does not matter

Correct answer: C

Per-answer feedback: - A: Incorrect. Future tense (will arrive) does not match the narration of events that already happened in the story. - B: Incorrect. Either tense can work if used consistently, but past tense is more natural for retelling story events that are narrated in past tense. - C: Correct. The novel is written in past tense, and a paragraph retelling its events should stay in past tense throughout. - D: Incorrect. Consistency matters: switching tenses mid-paragraph confuses the reader.

Consistent Verb Tense

Question: Which revision fixes the tense shift in this sentence? Original: "Marguerite entered the Chat Gris and asks Brogard about the tall Englishman."

- A. Marguerite enters the Chat Gris and asks Brogard about the tall Englishman. - B. Marguerite entered the Chat Gris and asked Brogard about the tall Englishman. - C. Marguerite entering the Chat Gris and asks Brogard. - D. Marguerite will enter the Chat Gris and asks Brogard.

Correct answer: B (primary; see note below)

Per-answer feedback: - A: Correct (also acceptable). Both verbs use present tense: consistent. - B: Correct. Both verbs use past tense, matching the novel's narration: consistent. - C: Incorrect. Entering is a participle, not a complete verb; this creates a sentence fragment. - D: Incorrect. Will enter is future tense; asks is present tense. The sentence is still inconsistent.

Canvas setup note for Q8: Both A and B are valid corrections. If Canvas allows multiple correct answers, mark both A and B as full credit. If the quiz must have a single correct answer, use B (past tense) as the primary correct answer, since past tense matches the novel's narration.

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 6: Commas in Complex Sentences and Dialogue Punctuation)

questions.text: Which sentence correctly punctuates a complex sentence where the dependent clause comes first?

answers.text: When Marguerite heard Chauvelin's voice she felt her blood run cold.
When Marguerite heard Chauvelin's voice, she felt her blood run cold.
Marguerite felt, her blood run cold when she heard Chauvelin's voice.
When Marguerite heard Chauvelin's voice she felt, her blood run cold.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The dependent clause "When Marguerite heard Chauvelin's voice" comes first, so a comma follows it before the independent clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the subordinating conjunction. If the clause it begins comes first in the sentence, a comma separates it from the independent clause.

questions.text: What is the correct term for words like "although," "because," "when," and "as soon as" that begin a dependent clause?

answers.text: article adjectives
conjunctions that connect independent clauses only
subordinating conjunctions
subject pronouns

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Subordinating conjunctions begin dependent clauses and connect them to an independent clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: These words do connect clauses, but they begin the dependent (partial) clause. They are subordinating conjunctions.

questions.text: Read this sentence: "Although Chauvelin was angry, he pretended to be calm." Which part is the independent clause?

answers.text: Although Chauvelin was angry
he pretended to be calm
Although Chauvelin
was angry, he pretended

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "He pretended to be calm" is a complete sentence on its own -- a subject, a verb, and a complete thought.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The independent clause can stand alone as a complete sentence. "Although Chauvelin was angry" cannot stand alone.

questions.text: Which sentence does NOT need a comma because the independent clause comes first?

answers.text: Because she dared not move, Marguerite stayed hidden.
She stayed hidden because she dared not move.
Although Percy saw Chauvelin, he showed no fear.
If the soldiers arrived, all would be lost.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. When the independent clause comes first and the dependent clause follows, no comma is needed.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the sentence where the independent clause (the complete thought) comes before the subordinating conjunction.

questions.text: In the sentence "As soon as he is aware of his danger, he will exercise more caution," what is the subject pronoun of the independent clause?

answers.text: danger
soon
he
caution

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "He" is the subject pronoun of the independent clause. Ask "who or what will exercise?" and the answer is he.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask "who or what will exercise more caution?" That answer is the subject of the independent clause.

questions.text: Which of these correctly punctuates a line of dialogue followed by a speaker tag?

answers.text: "The very walls have ears," he said.
"The very walls have ears" he said.
"The very walls have ears", he said.
"The very walls have ears." He said.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The comma goes inside the closing quotation mark, and the speaker tag starts with a lowercase letter.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check where the comma sits relative to the quotation marks, and whether the speaker tag is capitalized.

questions.text: In the line of dialogue "Hush!" he said in genuine alarm -- what is the speaker tag?

answers.text: Hush!
he said in genuine alarm
in genuine alarm
said

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The speaker tag is the whole phrase that tells who spoke and how: "he said in genuine alarm."
questions.feedback_incorrect: The speaker tag is the full phrase that identifies the speaker and may describe how they spoke.

questions.text: Which line of dialogue is correctly punctuated?

answers.text: "I vow I never thought of meeting you here!" He exclaimed Percy.
"I vow I never thought of meeting you here!" Percy exclaimed.
"I vow I never thought of meeting you here"! Percy exclaimed.
"I vow I never thought of meeting you here!" Percy Exclaimed.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. The exclamation point goes inside the quotation marks, and the speaker tag ("Percy exclaimed") starts with an uppercase letter only because it begins a new sentence after the exclamation point.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look at where the exclamation point sits and whether the speaker tag is a new sentence or a continuation.

questions.text: A line of dialogue is split around the speaker tag: "I am so sorry," he said, "I seem to have upset you." Why does "I seem" begin with a capital I?

answers.text: Because it is a new speaker.
Because every word after a comma must be capitalized.
Because "I" is always capitalized as a pronoun, not because a new sentence begins.
Because the period after "said" ends the sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "I" is always written as a capital letter, but this second part of the speech is a continuation of the same sentence, not a new one.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check whether a period follows the speaker tag (which would make the second speech a new sentence) or a comma (which means it continues).

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a comma inside the quotation marks and a lowercase speaker tag?

answers.text: "We have an hour's start on him", she said hopefully.
"We have an hour's start on him." she said hopefully.
"We have an hour's start on him," she said hopefully.
"We have an hour's start on him" She said hopefully.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The comma belongs inside the closing quotation mark, and "she" is lowercase because the speaker tag continues the sentence.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check the comma position (inside or outside the quotation marks) and the capitalization of the speaker tag.

quizzes.title: Grammar POP! Quiz (Week 7: Misplaced and Dangling Modifiers + Proofreading and Editing)

questions.text: A modifier that is in the sentence but points to the wrong word is called:

answers.text: a dangling modifier
a misplaced modifier
a linking verb
a dependent clause

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A misplaced modifier is in the sentence but sits next to the wrong word, so it accidentally describes something unintended.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dangling modifier has no correct word to attach to at all. When the modifier is there but in the wrong spot, it is misplaced.

questions.text: Read this sentence: "Creeping through the hedge, the footsteps of Desgas were loud in the darkness." What is wrong with it?

answers.text: The subject and verb do not agree.
There is a comma splice.
The opening phrase "Creeping through the hedge" has no correct subject to attach to.
Nothing is wrong with it.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Footsteps cannot creep. The phrase dangles because the person who is creeping (Marguerite) is not named as the subject. Fix: Creeping through the hedge, Marguerite heard the loud footsteps of Desgas.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask who is creeping through the hedge. Can footsteps creep? The phrase has no correct noun to attach to in the sentence.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly places the modifier?

answers.text: Marguerite nearly ran a league to reach the hut.
Marguerite ran nearly a league to reach the hut.
Running the hut was reached by Marguerite nearly a league.
Marguerite ran a league nearly to reach the hut.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Nearly" sits directly before "a league," the thing it modifies. The sentence is clear: she ran a distance of almost one league.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Nearly" should sit right before the word it describes. In option A it seems to modify "ran," which would mean she almost ran but did not quite. That is not the intended meaning.

questions.text: In proofreading, you check that the subject and verb agree. Which of these sentences has a subject-verb agreement error?

answers.text: The soldiers obeyed every order Chauvelin gave.
Percy and Marguerite was reunited on the cliffs.
Chauvelin gave his men a sharp command.
The Daydream sailed safely toward England.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Percy and Marguerite" is a plural subject (two people), so the verb should be "were," not "was."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the subject of each sentence and ask: is it singular or plural? The verb must match.

questions.text: Read this sentence: "Hearing the voice singing, the trap was almost complete." What type of modifier error is this?

answers.text: Misplaced modifier
Dangling modifier
Subject-verb agreement error
Pronoun-antecedent error

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Who is hearing the voice? The trap cannot hear. The participial phrase "Hearing the voice singing" has no correct subject in the sentence to attach to. It dangles.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check whether the opening phrase has a correct noun to attach to in the sentence. Can a trap hear a voice?

questions.text: Which sentence is correctly proofread and has no errors?

answers.text: Running down the cliff, the rocks were slippery under Marguerite's feet.
Marguerite, running down the cliff, found the rocks slippery under her feet.
Running down the cliff, the slippery rocks were under Marguerite.
Marguerite ran down, the cliff's rocks slippery under her feet.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. "Running down the cliff" attaches clearly to Marguerite, the subject noun that follows. Subject and verb agree. The sentence is clean.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In option A and C, the phrase "Running down the cliff" points to the rocks, which cannot run. In option D, a comma joins two full clauses incorrectly (a comma splice).

questions.text: What is the term for a pronoun that does not match the noun it replaces in number?

answers.text: A dangling pronoun
A misplaced pronoun
A pronoun-antecedent error
A linking pronoun

questions.feedback_correct: Right. When a pronoun does not match its antecedent (the noun it replaces) in number or person, it is a pronoun-antecedent error.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The noun a pronoun refers back to is called its antecedent. When pronoun and antecedent do not match, that is the error name.

questions.text: Which sentence contains a pronoun-antecedent error?

answers.text: Chauvelin watched Marguerite, and he felt no pity for her.
Each soldier had their own post to guard on the cliff.
The soldiers raised their rifles when the order was given.
Marguerite wept with relief when she heard Percy's voice.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Each soldier" is singular ("each" always is), so the pronoun should be "his" to match. "Their" is plural and does not agree with "each soldier."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the noun a pronoun replaces. "Each" is always singular. Does the pronoun in the sentence match in number?

questions.text: In Chapter 31, Marguerite realizes that Percy had been disguised as:

answers.text: Armand's cell guard

questions.text: In Chapter 29, when Chauvelin's soldiers rush the hut, they find it empty because:

answers.text: Percy had hidden the fugitives in the cart
The fugitives had already escaped by boat before the trap closed

questions.text: Which word from this week's reading means "impossible to satisfy, pacify, or persuade"?

answers.text: peremptory
ubiquitous
supposition
implacable

questions.feedback_correct: Right. "Implacable" means impossible to calm or appease. Chauvelin's implacable hatred for the Pimpernel drives the whole novel's conflict.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the word that describes a hatred or anger that nothing can soften. Which of these fits that meaning?

questions.text: Read this sentence: "Rushing down the cliff path, the sea came into view." What is wrong with this sentence?

answers.text: The subject and verb do not agree.
The opening phrase has no correct subject to attach to.
"Rushing" is the wrong verb tense.
Nothing is wrong with this sentence.

questions.feedback_correct: Right. The sea cannot rush down a path. The participial phrase "Rushing down the cliff path" has no correct noun to attach to in the sentence; it dangles. A fix: "Rushing down the cliff path, Marguerite caught sight of the sea."
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask yourself: who is rushing down the cliff path? Can a sea rush? The phrase needs a subject that can actually perform the action.

questions.text: Which of these sentences is correctly written (no modifier errors, no agreement errors)?

answers.text: Chauvelin nearly reached the creek with all his soldiers in pursuit.
Reaching the creek, the Daydream was already moving.
Marguerite, exhausted and barefoot, stumbled toward the waiting boat.
Each of the fugitives raised their arms in relief when they saw Percy.

questions.feedback_correct: Yes. Option C is clean: "exhausted and barefoot" correctly modifies Marguerite, the subject. No dangling phrase, no agreement problem, no modifier error.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each option: in option A, "nearly" is a misplaced modifier (she nearly ran, or she ran nearly to the creek?). In option B, the Daydream cannot reach the creek. In option D, "each" is singular and "their" is plural.

questions.text: The word "peremptory" (Chapter 28) means:

answers.text: Lasting only a short time
Present everywhere at once
Insisting on immediate obedience; sharp in tone
Based only on a guess or assumption

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A peremptory command is one that demands instant obedience and allows no argument. Chauvelin speaks to his men in a peremptory tone throughout the novel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think about the way Chauvelin gives orders. What kind of tone would match a command like "Silence! Not a word!" when given to soldiers?

questions.text: At the end of Chapter 30, after the soldiers have gone to the wrong creek, Chauvelin:

answers.text: Returns to France immediately and abandons the chase
Realizes Percy was the cart driver and pursues him alone
Leaves Marguerite unconscious on the cliff with the bound Jew
Sends a messenger to Paris to report his failure

questions.feedback_correct: Right. Chauvelin leaves Marguerite unconscious (she was thrown down and gagged a second time) with the bound Jew on the cliff. He has been deceived by the false note and sent his soldiers in the wrong direction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: What does the text say Chauvelin does after he realizes he has been tricked? Look at the very end of Chapter 30.

questions.text: A conclusion paragraph in an argument essay should:

answers.text: Introduce new evidence that was not discussed in the body paragraphs
Restate the claim in fresh words, present the strongest evidence, and acknowledge a complication
Simply repeat the introduction paragraph word for word
Ask a new question that the essay has not tried to answer

questions.feedback_correct: Right. A strong conclusion restates the argument in new language, confirms the most important evidence, and shows the writer is honest about what complicates the claim. It does not introduce completely new evidence or copy the introduction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A conclusion closes the argument; it does not open new ones. What does a well-written conclusion do with the claim and the evidence already presented?

questions.text: Which sentence is the best thesis for an essay arguing that the Pimpernel's disguise is heroic?

answers.text: The Scarlet Pimpernel uses a disguise to rescue people from the guillotine during the French Revolution.
The Pimpernel's disguise is heroic because it requires the courage to be seen as worthless in order to save lives.
The Pimpernel is a brave man who loves his wife.
Baroness Orczy wrote a novel about a hero who hides his identity.

questions.text: Which sentence is an explanation, not just a retelling of evidence?

answers.text: In Chapter 10, Percy pretends to be interested only in fashion and acts bored when serious things are discussed.
Percy Blakeney is the Scarlet Pimpernel and he keeps his identity secret from his wife.
This moment shows that the kind of courage Orczy values requires letting the person you love think the worst of you in order to protect her.
There are many chapters in the novel where Percy uses his disguise to fool Chauvelin.

questions.text: Which sentence performs Move 1 of a counterargument correctly?

answers.text: However, Percy keeps the secret to protect Marguerite, which is itself an act of love.
It is true that the deception causes Marguerite real pain throughout the novel.
One could argue that the disguise is deceptive because it requires lying to the one person whose trust matters most to Percy.
In conclusion, the disguise is heroic because the mission could not succeed without it.

questions.text: Which sentence performs Move 3 of a counterargument correctly?

answers.text: A reader might say the Pimpernel is deceptive because he deceives even his allies.
That is a fair point. The novel does show that secrecy has costs for the people Percy cares about.
However, Orczy frames the secrecy as a condition of survival: exposure would mean arrests and executions, not just embarrassment.
The Pimpernel uses his disguise many times across the novel.

questions.text: Which of the following is a strong conclusion sentence?

answers.text: In conclusion, I have shown that the disguise is heroic because of courage, evidence, and the counterargument.
The Pimpernel's disguise is heroic because it requires moral courage.
Orczy suggests that heroism is not always recognized as heroism at the time: the bravest act in the novel goes unseen by almost everyone who witnesses it.
Chauvelin tries to catch the Pimpernel and uses Marguerite to do it.

questions.text: A student writes this evidence point: "Marguerite is sad because Percy ignores her." What is missing?

answers.text: A chapter number in parentheses
An explanation sentence that says what the detail shows about courage and disguise
A direct quote from the novel
A connection to Chauvelin

questions.text: Which of the following would NOT belong in an argumentative essay outline?

answers.text: A thesis that names a position and gives a reason
A list of every event in the novel, chapter by chapter
Two evidence points, each with an explanation
A counterargument with three moves

questions.text: My outline document includes a clearly labeled Thesis section with one sentence that takes a position, names a kind of courage, and gives a reason from the novel.

answers.text: True: my thesis does all three things
False: my thesis is missing one or more of those elements

questions.text: My outline includes a Counterargument section with all three moves: the other side stated fairly, something granted, and a response explaining why my argument still holds.

answers.text: True: all three moves are present
False: one or more moves are missing

quizzes.description: The reading and the project work for Module 6 are finished. This survey looks back on the module and shows the teacher what landed and what to revisit.

questions.text:
The Module Question, your refined answer. Look back at how you answered this in the Module Intro: **Heroism in disguise: what kind of courage does the novel celebrate, and when is it right to risk everything for strangers?

Answer it again now, in three or four sentences, using something specific from the novel (for example, the Pimpernel disguising himself as a cart driver to rescue a family, Marguerite's decision to cross to France to warn him, or the League members who follow him without knowing his name). How has your answer changed since the start?

(Survey, no scoring. Compare to the Q1 intro response to see growth.)

Confidence rating. How confident do you feel that you can make an argument about the kind of courage the novel celebrates and back it up with details from the book, including a thesis, evidence, and a counterargument?

answers.text: Very confident
Mostly confident
Somewhat confident
Not yet confident

questions.text:
What still feels unclear. Name one thing about The Scarlet Pimpernel, the theme of heroism and disguise, or the argument-writing skills in this module that still feels unclear or that you would like more practice with. If everything feels clear, say what you found hardest.

(Survey, free response. Teachers scan for common confusion points.)

Virtue reflection. Optima names seven virtues: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. The Scarlet Pimpernel is a story about a person who risks everything for strangers. Pick the ONE virtue the Pimpernel most clearly shows in the novel, and that this module asked of you:

answers.text: Courage (facing real danger, again and again, for people he does not know)
Service (putting others first, even at the cost of his own reputation and marriage)
Perseverance (continuing the mission even when Chauvelin closes in and the odds narrow)
Another of the seven virtues

discussions.title: Module Discussion: The Outsiders
discussions.html:
Loyalty, the divide, and staying gold in The Outsiders.

The reading so far covers the climax and what the novel says about the greasers and the Socs, about loyalty, and about holding on to something worth keeping. The novel asks whether the things that divide these two groups are as solid as they first appear, and whether what holds people together can reach across those lines.

Your post (one short paragraph): State one claim about what The Outsiders says about loyalty, the greaser-Soc divide, or what it means to stay gold. Then explain why you believe it, using one specific event or situation from the novel described in your own words (no direct quotation needed). For example, you might claim that the novel shows the divide between the groups is more about circumstance than character, and then describe a moment where the two sides behave in a way that looks more alike than different.

Your reply (to one classmate): Read one classmate's claim. Do you agree with their reasoning? If you agree, add a second example from the novel that strengthens it. If you disagree, explain respectfully where you think it falls short, using the novel.

Keep your post to about five to seven sentences. Keep your reply to two or three.

Posting rules

  • Post your own claim first, before you can see classmates' posts (set the Canvas option to require an initial post).
  • Use at least one specific event or situation from the reading, described in your own words.
  • Be respectful in disagreement. Argue with the idea, not the person.

discussions.title: Module Discussion: A Midsummer Night's Dream
discussions.html:
Everyone tells a story about the night in the wood.

Theseus dismisses the lovers' account of their night in the wood as the raving of "the lunatic, the lover, and the poet," and Hippolyta answers that the story "grows to something of great constancy." Egeus narrates Lysander's courtship as a kind of theft, Titania explains the ruined seasons as the result of her quarrel with Oberon, and Bottom gives up entirely on describing his own vision. Everyone in this play tells a story about what happened. Not all of the stories agree, and not all of them match what the audience actually saw.

Your post (one short paragraph): Choose one character's account of the night in the wood. State one claim about whether that account can be trusted, and why. Support your claim with one specific moment from the play, cited in MLA format (Shakespeare's name plus act.scene). For example, you might claim that Egeus's account of Lysander is unreliable because it is delivered as a formal complaint meant to win a ruling, not as a neutral report, and cite the moment where he asks for "the ancient privilege of Athens" (Shakespeare, 1.1).

Your reply (to one classmate): Read one classmate's claim about a different character's account. Do you agree with their reasoning? If you agree, add a second example from the play that strengthens it. If you disagree, explain respectfully where you think it falls short, citing the play.

Keep your post to about five to seven sentences. Keep your reply to two or three.

Posting rules

  • Post your own claim first, before you can see classmates' posts (set the Canvas option to require an initial post).
  • Use at least one specific moment from the play, cited in MLA format (Shakespeare's name plus act.scene).
  • Be respectful in disagreement. Argue with the idea, not the person.

discussions.title: Module 5 Discussion: Short Story Unit
discussions.html:
What makes the suspense in "The Most Dangerous Game" work?

Rainsford spends the entire hunt not knowing exactly where Zaroff is, what traps are ahead, or whether his plans will hold. But the reader knows more than Rainsford does in some moments, and less in others.

Post (one short paragraph): Make one claim about what creates the most suspense in this story: is it what we are told, or what we are not told? Then explain your reasoning using one specific moment from the story. For example, a post might claim that the suspense comes from what the reader does not know about the jungle layout, and then point to the scene where Rainsford sets his first trap in the dark.

Reply (to one classmate): Read one classmate's claim and decide whether the reasoning holds. If in agreement, add a second moment from the story that supports their point. If in disagreement, explain respectfully where you think it falls short, using the story.

Post: about five to seven sentences. Reply: two or three.

Posting rules

  • Post an original claim first, before classmates' posts are visible (set the Canvas option to require an initial post).
  • Use at least one specific moment from the story. A claim with no evidence is not finished.
  • Be respectful in disagreement. Argue with the idea, not the person.

discussions.title: Module Discussion: The Scarlet Pimpernel
discussions.html:
When is it right to risk everything for strangers?

In Chapter 1 of The Scarlet Pimpernel, you meet the Paris barricades during the Reign of Terror, where families are being sent to the guillotine daily. You also hear about a mysterious figure, an English stranger, who keeps slipping through the guards to rescue people he does not know and has no legal obligation to help. The crowd calls him supernatural. The French government calls him a criminal. The people he rescues call him their only hope.

Your post (one short paragraph): Make one claim about when, or whether, it is right to risk your own safety for people you do not know. You might argue that there are clear situations where courage requires it, or that such a choice can only be right if you count the cost honestly, or that loyalty to your own family or country comes first. State your position clearly, and explain the reasoning behind it. You do not need to quote the novel directly since you are only two chapters in, but you may refer to what you have read.

Your reply (to one classmate): Read one classmate's claim. Do you agree with their reasoning? If you agree, add one further condition or piece of reasoning that strengthens it. If you disagree, explain respectfully where you think it falls short.

Keep your post to about five to seven sentences. Keep your reply to two or three.

Posting rules

  • Post your own claim first, before you can see classmates' posts (set the Canvas option to require an initial post).
  • State a real position. A post that says only "it depends" without saying on what is not finished.
  • Be respectful in disagreement. Argue with the idea, not the person.
